Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 3:

﴿A Book﴾. This is also reported from al-Zajjaj and al-Hawfi. On the earlier possibilities it is either a substitute (badal) for it, or another predicate, or a predicate of an omitted subject. The clause ﴿whose verses are made distinct﴾ is, on all the possibilities, in the position of a qualifier (sifah) for "a Book". The attribution of the sending down (tanzil) to ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, from among His names, the Exalted, is to signal that it is the axis of religious and worldly benefits, occurring in accordance with the requirement of Divine mercy, as indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya approx. 21:107]. The making distinct of its verses (tafsil ayatihi) means distinguishing them verbally by their endings (fawasil), their cadences (maqatie), and the beginnings and ends of the surahs; and in meaning, by being promise, threat, narratives and rulings, and so on. Indeed, to the most just of scholars it is clear that there is no book at the beginning of creation that has gathered within it such diverse sciences and topics, in expression and in allusion, as the Qur'an does.

On the authority of al-Suddi: ﴿whose verses are made distinct﴾, meaning they were explained, so He distinguished between its lawful and unlawful, its prohibition and command, its promise and threat. Al-Hasan said: they were made distinct by promise and threat. Sufyan said: by reward and punishment. What we mentioned first is more general, and perhaps what they mentioned is by way of example rather than restriction. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that its verses were made distinct in the sending down, i.e., they were not sent down all at once; but this is not the right view.

It was read as "fassalat" (فَصَلَّتْ) with an open fa' and sad, lightened, meaning they separated truth from falsehood. Ibn Zayd said: between the Prophet (ﷺ) and whoever opposed him. This is on the basis that "faṣala" is transitive, or that "faṣala" (fa-ṣala) means it separated some of it from some other by the variation of its endings and meanings, on the basis that "faṣala" is intransitive, meaning "infaṣala" (separated), as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and when the caravan departed (fasalat al-'ir)﴾ [Yusuf 12:94].

It was also read as "fuṣilat" (فُصِلَتْ) with a dammed fa' and a kasred sad, lightened, as a passive, and the meaning is as already explained. ﴿An Arabic Qur'an﴾ is in the accusative by way of praise, with the implied verb "I mean" or "I praise" or the like; or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is said that it is a state of "a Book", since it is specified by the qualifier; and it is said that it is a state of "its verses". It was permitted for this state to be emphasizing of itself, and to be a preparation (muwatti'ah) for the state that follows it. It has also been said that it is accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., they recite it as a Qur'an. Al-Akhfash said: it is a second object of "fussilat". This, as you see, is so if you are not al-Akhfash. Whichever it is, in ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ there is an expression of favour regarding the ease of its recitation and understanding, since it was sent down in the tongue of the one to whom it was sent among his own people. ﴿For a people who know﴾, i.e., its meanings, since it is in their language; or the meaning is "for people of knowledge and reflection," on the basis that the verb is treated as intransitive. The lam in ﴿for a people﴾ is causal (ta'liliyyah) or of specification (ikhtisasiyyah). He specified them with this because they are the ones who benefit from it. The prepositional phrase is either in the position of another qualifier for "Qur'an", or a complement (silah) for "sending down", or for "fussilat". Al-Zamakhshari said: it cannot be a qualifier like what precedes and follows it, i.e., "an Arabic Qur'an, existing for an Arab people", lest a separation be made between complements and qualifiers. Perhaps he meant, lest it entail separating the qualifier from what it qualifies, which is

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a bearer of glad tidings and a warner﴾, and the noun it describes, which is (a Qur'an). This is on the basis that it is an attribute (sifah) of it through the prepositional phrase (silah), which is (for a people), on the assumption that it is connected to (revelation), or to (its verses were detailed). Between the prepositional phrase and what it modifies, and between the attribute and its noun, there is a separation. That is, (a revelation) or (its verses were detailed, for a people). The plural is for emphasis, in the manner of your saying to someone who is separating two others: "Do not do it, for separating brothers is blameworthy." Or he intended, lest he separate the two relative clauses in the ruling, when there is no reason for separation. That is, the phrase ﴿from the Most Merciful﴾ connects to its relative clause, while ﴿for a people﴾ does not connect to it. Likewise between the two attributes: (Arabic) connects to its noun, while (bashiran) does not connect to it. The plural is for this reason too.

Abu Hayyan chose that the prepositional phrase be a relative clause of (fussilat). He said: "Its connection to (revelation) is remote, because it was described before its complement was taken, if ﴿from the Most Merciful﴾ is in the position of an attribute, or was made a substitute for (a Book), or was a predicate of (revelation). In that case there would be a substitution from the relative clause, or a predication about it before taking its complement, and that is not permissible." Perhaps that is not unanimously agreed upon. That (bashiran) is an attribute of (a Qur'an) is the well-known view. It is also permitted that it, together with what is conjoined to it, be a circumstantial clause (hal) from (a Book) or from (its verses). Zayd ibn Ali read "bashirun" and "nadhirun" with the nominative case, and this is an anomalous narration from Nafi', as an attribute of (a Book), or as a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is a bearer of glad tidings to the people of obedience and a warner to the people of disobedience. ﴿But most of them turned away﴾ from reflecting upon it and accepting it. The pronoun refers to (a people) on the first meaning, and to the disbelievers previously mentioned on the second meaning. It is also permissible that it refers to (a people) on this view too, by intending by it those whose nature is knowledge and reflection. ﴿So they do not hear﴾, that is, they do not accept and do not obey. From your saying: "I interceded with so-and-so, but he did not hear my words," though he did hear them, but since he did not accept them and did not act according to their requirement, it is as if he had not heard them. This is a well-known metaphor.

In al-Kashshaf: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿turned away﴾ corresponds to His saying, ﴿for a people who know﴾, and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿so they do not hear﴾ corresponds to His saying, majestic is His glory, ﴿a bearer of glad tidings and a warner﴾. That is, they denied its inimitability and did not submit to it despite knowing it, and they did not accept its glad tidings and its warnings, because they did not reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 5:**

﴿And they say: "Our hearts are in coverings"﴾, meaning thick coverings, ﴿from what you call us to﴾, namely belief in Allah alone and abandoning what we found our fathers upon. "Min" (from) here is used for the inception of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya), in the sense of what is in the sea. ﴿And in our ears is a deafness﴾, meaning deafness; its root meaning is heaviness.

Talha read it with a kasra on the waw, and it is also read with a fatha on the qaf. ﴿And between us and you there is a barrier﴾, a thick one that prevents us from communicating. The "min" here indicates that the barrier begins from both sides, such that it fills the intervening distance entirely, and no empty space remains between them at all.

Its clarification is that al-bayn (the space between), in the sense of the middle, is pronounced with a sukun. When it is said, "Between us and you is a barrier," it is true of a barrier located between the two of them that fills the whole space. But when it is said, "from between us" (min baynina), it indicates that the beginning of the barrier is from the middle, namely its end which is near the speaker. So whether "min" is repeated or not, the other end is an endpoint from one aspect and a beginning from another. Thus the apparent meaning is the filling of the whole, because the entire direction, namely the space between, was made the starting point of the barrier, so the endpoint is definitely something else. This suffices to distinguish the two forms. Moreover, al-bayn has been repeated to resume the beginning from that direction too, for if it had been said "and from between us," with the speaker given precedence, it would have sufficed. Furthermore, the necessity of coordination with something like "bayni wa baynika" (between me and you), if granted, does not contradict the intention of repeating it, so reflect upon this.

What they mentioned, the three sentences, are illustrations of the averseness of their hearts from grasping and accepting the truth, the rejection of their ears to it, and the impossibility of their connecting with and agreeing with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). By this they intended to make him despair (iqnat) of their following him, peace and blessings be upon him, so that he would not call them to the straight path.

Abu Hayyan mentioned that since the heart is the seat of knowledge, and the hearing and sight are aids in acquiring knowledge, they stated that these three are screened from anything painful that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) might convey to them. They said "on our hearts are coverings" just as they said "and in our ears is a deafness," so that the speech would be of one pattern in making the hearts and the ears the place of settlement of the coverings and the deafness. Although one of them is a settling of elevation (isti'la') and the other a settling of containment (ihtiwa'), since there is no difference in meaning between "our hearts are in coverings" and "on our hearts are coverings." The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it﴾ [al-Kahf: 57]. If it were said, "Indeed, We have placed their hearts in coverings," the meaning would not differ. So the correspondence (mutabaqa) is achieved in terms of meaning, and the Arabs, who are eloquent speakers, do not observe correspondence and consideration except in meanings. The specific placement of each of the two expressions in its position is for variety of style. Furthermore, since it was attributed to Allah, exalted is He, in surat Bani Isra'il and al-Kahf, the meaning of elevation and subjugation was more fitting, whereas here, since it is a report of their statement, the meaning of containment is closer. So did some of the eminent scholars verify it, and they hinted at a reservation about it.

The interpretation of al-akinna (coverings) as "coverings" (aghita') is what most of the exegetes adopt. Thus it is the plural of kinan, like ghita' both in wording and meaning. It was also said: they are what arrows are placed in (quiver). Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid that he said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: "Our hearts are in coverings"﴾, that they said, "like a quiver for arrows." ﴿So work﴾ according to your religion, and it was said: in nullifying our affair. ﴿Indeed, we are working﴾ according to our religion, and it was said: in nullifying your affair. The statement according to the first interpretation is a disengagement and a despairing of following him, peace and blessings be upon him. Their intention is "indeed we are working," and the first is a preparation for it. The essential meaning is: we do not abandon our religion, rather we remain steadfast upon it,
*Page 97*
just as you remain steadfast upon your religion. According to the second interpretation, it is a challenge in opposition and dispute. The one who said what was mentioned was Abu Jahl, and with him a group of the Quraysh.

There is a report that Abu Sahl al-Sarri transmitted through the chain of Abd al-Quddus, from Nafi' ibn al-Azraq, from Ibn Umar, from Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said regarding the verse: "The Quraysh came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to them: 'What prevents you from Islam, so that you may lead the Arabs?' They said: 'O Muhammad, we do not understand what you say, and we do not hear it, and indeed on our hearts are thick coverings (ghulf).' Abu Jahl took a garment and pulled it, so that between it and the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, was (a distance), and he said: 'O Muhammad, our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is a deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier.'" And in it: "When it was the next day, seventy men of them came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, present Islam to us.' When he presented Islam to them, they all embraced Islam. The Prophet (ﷺ) smiled and said: 'Praise be to Allah! Yesterday you claimed that on your hearts were thick coverings, and your hearts are in coverings from what I call you to, and in your ears is a deafness, and today you have become Muslims.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we lied, by Allah. Yesterday, had we been like that, we would never have been guided. But Allah, exalted is He, is the Truthful, and the servants are the liars against Him. He is the Self-Sufficient, and we are the needy toward Him.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 6:

﴿Say, "I am only a man like you."﴾ I am not an angel nor a jinn, such that you could not receive from him. This is a rebuttal of their saying: "Between us and you is a barrier." ﴿It is revealed to me that your God is but one God.﴾ That is: I do not call you to what the intellects recoil from; rather I call you to the tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) which the proofs of reason indicate and the evidences of revelation (al-sam') bear witness to. This is an answer to their saying: "Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness." ﴿So go straight to Him﴾: that is, stand upright toward Him, Exalted is He, with tawhid and sincerity in worship, and do not cling to the handholds of shirk, nor say to whoever calls you to tawhid: "Our hearts are in coverings..." etc.

﴿And seek His forgiveness﴾ for what has passed from you of speech and action. This is an aspect not devoid of beauty in connecting the command with what precedes it. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary): that is, I am not of a different kind from you, such that there would be between me and you a barrier and a separation that justifies the difference of deeds and religions, as your saying indicates: ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾. Rather, I am only a man like you, commanded in what I command you, since we have all been informed of tawhid with an address that unites me and you. For the address in "your God" (ilahukum) is reported speech encompassing all, not that it is an address from him, peace be upon him, to the disbelievers, as in "your likeness" (mathalukum). This is based on choosing the first aspect in ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾, and there is no harm in it from this direction; yes, there is deficiency in it from another direction. The author of al-Fara'id said: this is not an answer to their saying, since it does not require that it have an answer. Its sum is: "Do not leave them and what they profess," and their saying that is intended as a reason for leaving them. Even granting that it is an answer, what is meant by it is: "I am a man, so I cannot bring your hearts out of the coverings, remove the barrier from between us, or the deafness from the ears. But I am revealed to, and commanded to convey: ﴿that your God is but one God.﴾" The Imam (al-Razi) has a statement close to what was mentioned, within the scope of acceptance; and both statements are not adequate to the eloquence of the noble composition. Al-Zamakhshari made it an answer on the basis that the polytheists often hold, in rejecting prophethood, that its claimant is a human, whereas he must be an angel, and it is not permissible for him to be a human; therefore they do not give ear to the Messenger's words nor reflect upon them. So his saying, peace be upon him: "I am not an angel; I am only a man," is by way of turning the argument back upon them (al-qalb 'alayhim), not a response in kind (al-qawl bil-mujib), nor part of the wise method at all, as it was said: it is as if he, ﷺ, said: "What you hold on to in rejecting my prophethood, that I am a human, is precisely what validates my prophethood, since it is not fitting in wisdom that an angel be sent to you. This necessitates your acceptance, not rejection and extreme aversion."

His saying: ﴿It is revealed to me that your God is but one God﴾ is a preface to the purpose of the mission after establishing prophethood first in detail with His saying, Exalted is He: "Ha Mim," the verses, and in summary a second time with His saying: ﴿It is revealed to me﴾. Then it was said: ﴿that your God is but one God﴾ as an explanation of the purpose. So His saying ﴿It is revealed to me﴾ is brought as a preface, and in it is an allusion to the establishment of prophethood. This meaning, on the view that what is meant by ﴿So act﴾ ... etc., is "act in the nullification of our affair, indeed we are acting in the nullification of your affair," is evident. As for the first view, its aspect is that religion is the totality of what the one sent is bound to: obedience to the Sender, Exalted is He, through the mediation of the messenger's conveyance. Thus it is consequent upon his prophethood, which is consequent upon its proof. By this they showed that they submit to what their forefathers had established among them concerning the incompatibility of prophethood with humanity, and that this is their religion; so it was said to them what was said. This aspect is more congruent and more eloquent. This is a fine and subtle point, though what was mentioned first comes to mind more quickly. In al-Kashshaf: ﴿Say, "I am only a man like you, it is revealed to me"﴾ corresponds to their denial of the miracle and prophethood, and His saying ﴿So go straight﴾ corresponds to non-acceptance. There is in this an allusion to something of what you have heard, so reflect.

Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read (qala innama) as a past-tense verb, and al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash read "yuhi" with a kasra on the ha', as an active form, meaning: God reveals to me that your God is but one God.

﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾ because of their shirk with their Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 7:

﴿Those who do not give the zakah⁠﴾ due to their stinginess and their lack of compassion for creation, and this is among the greatest vices. ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers⁠﴾: "they" is a subject (mubtada') and the predicate (khabar) follows; the second "they" (hum) is a separating pronoun (damir fasl). "In the Hereafter" (bil-akhirah) is connected to "disbelievers" (kafirun), and the fronting (taqdim) is for emphasis and for the sake of preserving the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fasilah). The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) indicating that their refusal to give zakah is due to their absorption in this world and their denial of the Hereafter. Interpreting zakah in its legal sense is what Ibn al-Sa'ib said, and it is reported from Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Muqatil. It has also been said: zakah is taken in its linguistic sense, i.e., they do not do that which purifies their souls, which is faith and obedience.

It is reported from Mujahid and al-Rabi' that the meaning is: they do not purify their deeds. Ibn Jarir and a group related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "In that" means they do not say "There is no god but Allah," and likewise al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and others related it from 'Ikrimah. The meaning then is: they do not purify themselves from shirk. Al-Tibi chose this view and said: the meaning according to it is "so be upright toward Him with monotheism and sincere worship of Him, the Exalted, and repent to Him, glorified is He, from what has preceded for you of shirk, and woe to you if you do not do all of that." So the prohibition of giving zakah was put in its place, to indicate that uprightness in monotheism, sincerity of deed for Allah, the Exalted, and disavowal of shirk is the purification of the soul. This is more fitting to the composition of the verse, and what the scholar of the Ummah (Ibn 'Abbas) held was only for the sake of observing the composition of the verse. And he made his saying:

The Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that is not cut off.﴾ That is, "not cut off." It is mentioned by way of digression (istitrad), as a veiled reference to the polytheists and to the fact that their share is cut off, since they did not (yuzakkū) purify themselves as the believers were purified. He cites the verse that follows as evidence for the digression. In al-Kashf, the first view is more apparent, and "the polytheists" remains on its general meaning. It is not a case of placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, as in this view. The sentence is parenthetical, like the reason for what He commanded them. Likewise, ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ and the verse is in the position of "Woe to the polytheists and blessed are the believers." Both contain warning and encouragement, which confirms that the command to faith and uprightness is an emphasis whose condition is not hidden from any person of intellect. Likewise, zakat in it is taken in its apparent sense. Among the attributes of the disbelievers, withholding it was singled out because it is a measure of the faith hidden in the heart. How so? It has been said: "Wealth is the twin of the soul." Indeed, some men of letters said:

They said, "Your soul's twin is your wealth, so guard it."
I replied, "Wealth is better than the soul."

I see that guarding it brings about the improvement of my state,
and squandering it leads to a shameful begging.

Diverting the term from its widespread legal meaning without a valid reason is not permissible. How so, when the meaning of "giving" (al-iti') does not stand firm? Yes, if the word in its place were "yatūna" (they come), as in His saying: ﴿And they do not come to prayer except while they are lazy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 54], it would be fine. It cannot be said that zakat was enjoined in Medina while the surah is Meccan, because we say: applying the name to a portion taken out of wealth, in a particular manner of devotion, was common before it became obligatory. This is shown by the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt: "Those who perform the zakat." Moreover, this particular ruling in this known form was made obligatory in Medina,
[Page 99]
but in Mecca some portion of wealth was made obligatory to be paid to the entitled recipient, though not in this form, and it too was called zakat, and then it was abrogated. End of quotation. From this it is known that what al-Tayyibi said is invalid. What remains is the opposition of the learned one (al-Habr), and that is only established if the report from him is established. After that the matter is also easy. Perhaps he, may Allah be pleased with him, used to read "lā yatūna" from ityān (coming), since the well-known reading rejects that except with a distant interpretation. It is strange that what was mentioned from the learned one in al-Bahr is attributed to the majority as well. Taking the verse in that sense is a way out for some who do not hold that disbelievers are charged with the subsidiary rulings, but the condition of such an interpretation is not hidden. Yet the verse, in its obvious meaning, is evidence against it. Among those who do not hold this view, one said: they are charged with believing in its truth, not with performing it, and the charge to perform it comes after faith. So the meaning of the verse is: "they do not give zakat after faith." It has also been said: the meaning is "they do not acknowledge its obligation." The view that the insane are charged is closer than this interpretation. It has been said that the word "woe" (wayl) indicates blame, not charge, and blame is rationally deserved. In this there is a discussion that is not hidden. This is what has been said. It has also been said regarding "mamnūn": "not reckoning favours upon them," from al-mann meaning the enumeration of blessings. Its original meaning is "burden," so it was applied to that because of its burden on the one upon whom it is bestowed. From Ibn Abbas, it is explained as "diminished." They recited for Dhu al-Isba' al-Adwani:

By your life, my door is not one with a lock
against the friend, nor is my provision diminished.

According to what is narrated from al-Suddi, the verse was revealed concerning the sick and the aged. When they are unable to perform the full acts of obedience, there is written for them, in sickness and old age, a reward like that which was written for them when they were healthy and young, and their rewards are not diminished. That is from the great generosity and mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 9:

﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days?﴾ up to the end of the verses. There is much to say about them, and some of it is not well known. Let us begin with what is well known, and after completing it we will mention the rest. So we say: this is a denial and a condemnation of their disbelief. The lam (la) is either for emphasizing the denial, and the hamza (alif of interrogation) is placed first because it demands initial position, not because it denies the emphasis. Or it is to indicate that their disbelief is so far-fetched that rational people would deny its occurrence, so it needs emphasis. God, glorified is He, linked their disbelief to the relative clause (al-mawsul) to magnify His majesty and to emphasize the enormity of their disbelief in Him, mighty and majestic is He. The apparent meaning is that "the earth" refers to the known body. It has been said: perhaps what is meant by it is what lies in the lower direction of the dense and subtle bodies, namely earth, water and air, used metaphorically by employing it for a necessary meaning, as has been said, by the indication of contrast. This interpretation was adopted so that the statement would not be silent about the duration of the creation of everything other than the earth. Among the meanings of His creating it in two days is that He, glorified is He, first created for it a common origin, then created for it forms through which it diversified into kinds. "Day" in common usage is an expression for the period during which the sun is above the horizon, but what is meant here is the time in general, because that cannot be conceived before the creation of the heavens, the stars and the earth itself. Then that period may be of the length of the known day, and it may be less or more than that; the lesser is more suitable to the context. Whatever the case, the apparent meaning is that the two days are the time frames for the creation of the earth absolutely, without distribution.

Some eminent scholars said: God created its origin and its substance in one day, and formed it and its layers in another day. In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (Guidance of the Sound Mind) it is said: what is meant by the creation of the earth is the determination of its existence, that is, He decreed that it would come into being in two days, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with God is as the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. What is meant by their disbelief in Him, may He be exalted, is their deviation regarding His essence, glorified is He, and His attributes, mighty and majestic is He, and their departure from the truth that is necessarily owed to Him by His servants, namely His unity and the belief in what befits His essence and attributes, majestic is His grandeur. They do not declare Him exempt from the attributes of bodies, nor do they affirm for Him complete power and the attributes fitting for Him, glorified and exalted is He. They do not acknowledge that He, exalted is He, sent the messengers, nor that He, glorified is He, resurrects the dead, to the extent that it is as if they claim that He, glorified is He, created the servants in vain and left them without purpose. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you set up rivals to Him﴾ is a conjunction with "you disbelieve," included with it in the ruling of denial and reproach. Making it a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "created" is of no concern. The plural of "rivals" (andad) is by consideration of what actually exists, not that the basis of the denial is plurality. That is: "and you set up for Him rivals and equals from among the angels, the jinn and others, while it is not possible that He, glorified is He, should have even one rival." ﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the relative clause, by consideration of its being characterized by what is in its complement, and the sense of distance in it, together with the recentness of the reference to what is indicated, to signal the loftiness of its rank in greatness. The kaf (the "-ka" of the demonstrative) is singular because what is intended is not to specify the addressees. It is the subject, and its predicate is what follows: that is, that Great One of exalted rank who did what has been mentioned within a short period. ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, the Creator of all existing things and their Sustainer, not of the earth alone. How then could it be conceived that any of His creatures should be a rival to Him, mighty and majestic is He?

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 41, verse 10:

As for His saying, ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains from above it﴾: according to what many scholars have chosen, it is a conjunction (*'atf*) with ﴿He created the earth﴾, and it falls under the ruling of the relative clause (*silah*). There is no harm in the separation between them by the two sentences mentioned, because the first is connected to His saying, ﴿you disbelieve (*takfurun*)﴾, in the position of its repetition, and the second is a parenthetical (*mu'tarida*) sentence confirming the meaning of the speech. So the separation by them is no separation at all. There is also eloquence in it in terms of meaning, since it indicates that the thing conjoined to (i.e., ﴿He created the earth﴾) is sufficient for His being the Lord of the worlds and for no rival being ascribed to Him, so how much more so when these conjoined elements are added to it.

It has been objected that the connection does not remove it from being an interruption that confuses the mind and produces complexity. Therefore, the correct and closest view is that the *waw* be considered parenthetical (*i'tiradiyyah*), and that each of the two sentences be a parenthesis, so that the parenthesis is cancelled by the parenthesis. Or it may be taken as the beginning of a new speech, on the basis that it may begin with *waw*. Or it may be said: it is conjoined to something implied, like ﴿He created﴾. The author of *al-Kashf* (al-Taybi) chose this last view, saying: "The most plausible thing said about it is that it is conjoined to something implied after ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: He created it and placed in it firm mountains. So it is as if He related His saying, ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾, first as a refutation of their disbelief, then mentioned it again as a completion of the account and an emphasis on the denial. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds﴾, is not in the manner of a parenthesis, such that the sentence would be conjoined to the relative clause, and the interruption of ﴿you set up (*taj'alun*)﴾ as a conjunction to ﴿you disbelieve﴾ would be excused by its unity with what precedes it, in the style of ﴿and turning away from the way of God, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. That is because it is intended for its own sake in this context and is a pillar of the denial, like His saying, ﴿in the One who created the earth﴾, and this is emphasized in a way that is not hidden from one of insight."

*Al-Rawasi* (the firm mountains) are the mountains, from *rasa* (to be fixed, firm). The intended meaning of "placing" is their actual bringing into existence. In *al-Irshad* (Abu al-Su'ud), the intended meaning is the decree of placing, not the placing itself as an actual act. His saying, ﴿from above it﴾, is connected to *ja'ala* (placed) or to something omitted as a qualifier of *rawasi*, meaning: existing from above it, with the pronoun referring to the earth. In this there is *istikhdam* (a rhetorical device in which a term is used in one sense and its pronoun in another), according to what has been said about its intended meaning, since the mountains are above the known earth and not above all the lower bodies and elemental simples. The benefit of ﴿from above it﴾ is to indicate that they were placed raised above it, not beneath it like pillars, nor fixed within it like nails, so that their benefits would be presented to its inhabitants and what they contain of places of consideration and fields of thought would become manifest to observers. By my life, the wisdom of their elevation is among the creative wisdoms that minds are astonished by. The verse does not preclude that there be mountains in the submerged part of the earth beneath the water, as is not hidden. And God Most High knows best.

﴿And He blessed in it﴾, that is, He multiplied its good. In *al-Irshad*: He decreed, glorified is He, that its good should increase by multiplying in it kinds of plants and kinds of animals, of which man is one. ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance (*aqwat*)﴾, that is, He set a proportion between its quantity and its measures. And in *al-Irshad* it says: that is, He decreed by action that there should be produced in what will come, for its inhabitants, the various kinds of their suitable sustenance, in a determined measure that wisdom requires. The speech is on the basis of an omitted genitive (*mudaf*). It has been said that this does not need it, and the attribution is due to the slightest connection. This is what the words of al-Suddi indicate when he said: "He attributed the sustenance to it from the standpoint that it is in it and emerges from it." Mujahid interpreted *aqwat* as rain and waters.

In another report from him, and to it went 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak, the meaning is what each region is specially given of clothing, food, and plants, so that people need one another. This requires the cultivation of the earth and the orderliness of the affairs of the world. This is supported by the recitation of some: "and He distributed in it its sustenance (*qassama*)." ﴿In four days﴾ is connected to the occurrence of the matters mentioned, not to their measuring, according to what is in *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*. The speech is on the basis of an omitted genitive, meaning: He decreed their occurrence within the completion of four days. Al-Zajjaj used to connect it to *qaddara* (decreed), as is the view of Imam Abu Hanifa regarding a qualifier that comes after a series of conjoined elements, like: "I honored Zayd, struck 'Amr, and saw Khalid in the house." Al-Shafi'i says: a qualifier that follows sentences refers back to all of them, because the basic principle is that the conjoined and the conjoined-to share in the complements. So the qualifier here refers to the placing of the mountains and what follows it, and this is what comes to my understanding. It is necessary to posit the genitive you have heard, and al-Zajjaj explicitly stated it. Al-Zamakhshari did not posit it, and made the preposition-phrase connected to an omitted element that occurs as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: all of that, from the creation of the earth and what follows it, exists within four days. This is on the basis that it is a *fadhlakah* (a summing-up), meaning a detached statement brought to summarize what was mentioned in detail, taken from the *fadhlakah* of calculation and the saying "*fadhlaka kadhā*" (that totals so-and-so) after the collection has been established. What is in our case included in it a number of a sum with another sum, and treating it so does not prevent the conjunction of ﴿He placed in it firm mountains﴾ to something implied, because the non-explicit linkage is sufficient. The claim that the summing-up requires explicit mention of both sentences, like saying: "I traveled from Basra to Wasit in two days, and from Wasit to Kufa in two days, so that totals four days," and here he specified only one of the two periods, is not sound, because knowledge of the two periods is sufficient for the realization of the summing-up, and the intention is that it is run in its manner. The reason the reading that the placing of the mountains and what is mentioned after it, or the measuring of the sustenance, is in four days was not permitted, is that it would require that the creation of the earth and what is in it be in six days, and it has been mentioned after that that the creation of the heavens was in two days, so the total would be eight days.

It has been repeatedly stated in the Book of God Most High that the creation of both of them, I mean the heavens and the earth, was in six days. The four days are qualified by His saying, ﴿equal (*sawa'an*)﴾. It is an infinitive of emphasis (*masdar mu'akkid*) for an implied verb that is a qualifier of *ayyam* (days), meaning: they became equal, *sawa'an* (equally), that is, equal balance, as is indicated by the recitation of Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, 'Isa, and Ya'qub, "*sawa'in*" with the genitive, for it is explicit in being a qualifier. By this the view that it is a circumstantial (*hal*) from the pronoun in ﴿their sustenance (*aqwatha*)﴾ is weakened, together with the rarity of a circumstantial from the genitive-noun in other than the three cases, and the necessity of the two recitations differing in meaning.

It is known from this that according to the recitation of Abu Ja'far with the nominative, it is taken as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is *sawa'un* (equal), and the sentence is also taken as a qualifier of *ayyam*, not a circumstantial from the pronoun, to avoid figurative usage. For it is common in such matters and consistent in the usage of Arabs and non-Arabs. You find them saying: "I did it in two days," and they mean in a day and a half, for example; and "I traveled four days," and they mean three and a half, for example. From it is His saying, ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], for the intended meaning of "months" there is Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the night of sacrifice. That is because the excess was made a single unit figuratively, and then the designation of the complete number was applied to the whole. So the meaning here is "in four days" without deficiency or excess. And it seems that for this reason what is in the revelation was preferred over saying: "He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed in it, and measured in it its sustenance, in two days," as has been said before: "He created the earth in two days." The point is that if it had been said so, it would be permissible to intend by the two days the first two and the last two, most of them. He did not say, "He created the earth in two full days, and placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed in it, and measured in it its sustenance in two full days," or "He created the earth in two days, and placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed in it, and measured in it its sustenance in two days," that totals four, equal. This is because what He, glorified is He, presented is more concise, more eloquent, and better suited to what the Revelation contains of the depths of minds and the strikes of the riding-beasts, so that the superior is distinguished from the deficient, the forward from the backward, degrees are raised, and rewards are multiplied.

Some eminent scholars said: in the sublime arrangement there is an indication, together with conciseness, that the last two days are connected to the first two days, since it is understood from making them one unit and their being connected in mention. His saying, ﴿for the seekers (*lil-sa'ilin*)﴾, is connected to an omitted element that occurs as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this restriction to four is for those who ask about the duration of the creation of the earth and what is in it. There is no harm in the successive omission of two subjects, on the basis of what al-Zamakhshari preferred regarding the preposition-phrase before it. It has been said that it is connected to the earlier *qaddara* (decreed), meaning: and He measured in it its sustenance for the sake of those who seek it, who need it, from those who feed on it. It has been said: it is connected to an implied element that is a circumstantial of the sustenance. All of these do not hold except according to what al-Zajjaj preferred, not what al-Zamakhshari preferred, because the summing-up, as is known from what preceded, cannot occur except after the completion of the two sentences, so it is not permissible for it to intervene between the second sentence and some of its complements. It has been said that it is connected to *sawa'* (equal), on the basis that it is a circumstantial from the pronoun, and the meaning is: equal, prepared for those in need. Or it is connected to it on the recitation of the nominative, taking it as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: that is, the matter of these created things and their benefit is equal, prepared for the human beings who need it. And this, as you see, is weak.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 11:

﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ means He directed Himself toward it and set His course for it, without intending any effect upon other things, from the expression "istawa ila makan kadha" (he went straight to such a place) when one heads toward it and does not turn aside to anything else.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) mentioned that istiwa', when it is followed by "ala" (upon), carries the sense of istila' (taking possession), as in His saying, ﴿The Most Merciful settled upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]. When it is followed by "ila" (to), it carries the sense of reaching a thing, either in essence or in management (tadbir). On the second usage is His saying, ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, and the rest of the verse. The statements of the early generation (al-salaf) concerning istiwa' are well known.

We have already mentioned some of this earlier. The apparent meaning of some scholars' words suggests that there is an omitted noun in the sentence, meaning: "Then He turned to the creation of the heaven, ﴿while it was smoke﴾, a dark matter. Perhaps by it is meant its substance from which it was composed. I do not hold the view of indivisible atoms (al-jawahir al-fardah), because of the strength of the evidences negating them, and no harm at all follows from that, as will not be hidden from the intelligent and fair-minded person." It has also been said: His Throne, exalted is He, was before the creation of the heavens and the earth upon the water, and Allah caused heat in the water, so foam and smoke rose up. As for the foam, it remained on the surface of the water, and Allah created dryness in it, and He, glorified is He, brought the earth from it. As for the smoke, it rose and ascended, and Allah created the heavens from it.

It has also been said: there was there a red ruby, and He, glorified is He, looked upon it with the eye of majesty, so it melted and became water, which foamed, and smoke rose from it, and so what happened happened. In any case, the smoke was not produced from fire, which is one of the elements, because fire is among the accessories of the earth, and it did not exist at that time according to one view, as you will know, God willing. And according to the view that it existed, no one has held that this was formed from that fire. The truth that should be followed, and nothing else considered, is that the sphere of fire which the early philosophers claim, and many people agreed with them upon, does not exist, and the occurrence of shooting stars does not depend on its existence, as is clear to one of sharp intellect.

﴿So He said to it and to the earth: Come, willingly or unwillingly﴾ — with what I have created in you of benefits. The meaning is not the coming of their essences and their bringing into existence, but the coming forth of what is in them of the aforementioned, in the sense of making it manifest. The command is for subjection (taskhir). It has been said that on this view it is necessary that what follows the making of the heavens seven, or the content of the whole group of sentences mentioned after the fa', be what is meant; otherwise the command to come in this sense follows the creation of the earth and the heaven.

Some have said: the speech is in inverted order, and the original is: "Then He turned to the heaven, ﴿while it was smoke﴾, so He decreed them seven heavens..." etc. "So He said to it and to the earth: Come..." etc. This is further from dispute, though it contradicts the apparent sense; or it means: "Be and come into being in a specific manner and at a determined time for each of you." So what is meant is the coming of their essences and their bringing into existence, and the command is for creation (takwin), on the basis that khalaqa, ja'ala, barakа and qaddara carry the meaning we have related from the guidance of sound reason. This is a beginning in explaining the manner of creation after explaining the manner of determination. Perhaps the specification of the explanation to what relates to the earth and what is in it is because explaining His care for the matter of those addressed, and arranging the foundations of their livelihood before their creation, is among what moves them to faith and restrains them from disbelief and rebellion. He specified istiwa' to the heaven, although the address that follows it is directed to both of them together, relying on mention of the determination of the earth and the determination of what is in it, as if it were said: "It was said to it and to the earth whose existence and the existence of what is in it was determined: Be and come into being." This is the view that the author of al-Irshad preferred, and others mentioned it as a possibility. He took the command to be an expression of the connection of His will, exalted is He, to their existence, a connection by action, by way of illustration, without there being any commander and commanded, as has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: (Be!) and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾, as an illustration of the inevitability of the effect of His power, exalted is He, upon them and the impossibility of their refusing it, not as an affirmation of willingness or unwillingness to them. Both are verbal nouns placed in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning obedient or unwilling. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: We come obedient﴾, meaning submissive, is an illustration of the full extent of their being affected by the divine power and their fulfilling what they were commanded, and a depiction that their existence, as they are, is proceeding in accordance with the requirement of perfect wisdom, for obedience indicates that, while unwillingness suggests the opposite. It has been said: ﴿ta'i'in﴾ is in the masculine sound plural form, though it is specific to rational beings, in consideration of their being in the position of address and answer; and there is no reason for the feminine when they speak of themselves, since the feminine is only in terms of wording.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 12 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾, is an explanation and detailing of the general creation of the heaven, which was expressed by the word "command" (amr). Its answer is not that it is an act following upon their creation. That is, He created them with an originating creation (khalq ibda'i) and perfected their affair as wisdom requires, in two periods. The pronoun in (hunna) may refer to "the heaven" according to its meaning, since it means "the heavens," and for this reason it was said that it is a collective noun (ism jam'). (Seven) is a circumstantial accusative (hal, a noun in the accusative describing the state of the pronoun). Or the pronoun is unspecified (mubham), and what follows it explains it, with (seven) being a specification (tamyiz, a noun in the accusative clarifying a vague term). It belongs to the pronoun even though it comes later in wording and rank, because this is permissible in specification, as in the example "rabbahu rajulan" (his Lord, a man), and this is an acceptable Arabic construction.

Abu Hayyan said: (seven) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and it is a delayed (muqaddarah) state. Some said: it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun. It was also said: it is a direct object (maf'ul bihi), and the implied meaning is "He decreed from them seven heavens." Al-Hawfi said: it is a second object (maf'ul thani), with the verb "qada" (decree) being taken in the sense of "making" (tasyir). The amount of time for the creation of the earth and of what is in it was not mentioned, being sufficient with its mention in explaining their measure.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾, is coordinated (ma'tuf) on (qada-hunna). That is, He created in each of them what it was prepared for, and wisdom required that there be in them angels, luminous bodies, and other things that none knows except God Exalted, as the words of al-Suddi and Qatadah imply. Thus "revelation" (wahy) is an expression for creation, like "command" (amr), and it is restricted by the same time-restriction that qualifies the preceding coordinated clause. Or it means that He revealed to the inhabitants of each of them His commands and assigned to them what suits them of obligations, as has been said. Thus revelation in its well-known sense among its various meanings is unrestricted from the mentioned restriction, or restricted by it in my view. The possibility of restriction and non-restriction also applies to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾, meaning from the stars, and they are in it, although they differ in height and depth according to what the apparent meaning requires. Or some of them are in it and some are above it, but because all of them appear shining upon it, it is correct to say that its adornment is by them. The turning to the first person plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) is to display greater care.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And as a protection﴾, it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq, a verbal noun in the accusative that emphasizes or specifies the verb) for an implied verb coordinated on His saying "adorned" (zayyanna). That is: "and We guarded it with a guarding." The pronoun refers to the heaven, and its protection is either from calamities or from the devils who eavesdrop on hearing, and this matter has already been discussed. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the lamps, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. It was also permitted that it is a direct object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), according to meaning, that is, coordinated on an object of purpose implied in the preceding speech, meaning "as an adornment and as a protection." There is no hiding that this is a distant artificiality that should not be asserted when the first reading is evident and easy, as Abu Hayyan indicated in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That﴾, is taken as a reference to all that was mentioned in its details. That is: ﴿that which has been mentioned is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning the One who is complete in power and complete in knowledge. Then the author of al-Irshad (Abu al-Su'ud) said, after what you have heard quoted from him: according to this, there is no indication in the noble verse of an order between the existence of the earth and the existence of the heaven. The order is only between the measuring, that is, the measuring of the existence of the earth and what is in it, and the existence of the heaven. But if the creating and what is coordinated upon it of the three verbs are taken in their apparent meanings, then they indicate that the creation of the earth and what is in it came first, and most commentators agree on this. You should not hide from yourself that interpreting those verbs as he interpreted them is contrary to the apparent meaning, as he himself acknowledges. Also, not directly addressing the creation of the earth and what is in it, as he addressed the creation of the heavens in the same way, does not fit the claim of concern which he indicated in explaining why the explanation was restricted to what concerns the earth and what is in it. Moreover, the creation of what is in it in actuality is not apparent from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth: come willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly﴾, especially since the earth was mentioned earlier independently, and what is in it was mentioned independently. So from "the earth" here, only that independent earth is understood, not it together with what is in it. The matter of the precedence or delay of the creation of the earth will come, God willing, for discussion later.

It was said: the coming (ityan) of the heaven means its coming into being, and the coming of the earth means that it becomes spread out (madhwwah, extended). In this there is a combination of two figurative meanings, since the emergence from non-existence and the spreading and leveling of the earth were compared to coming from another place. Regarding the validity of combining them there is discussion. Also, regarding whether the spreading (dahw) is delayed after the placing of the mountains, there is discussion as well, which you will know God willing. It was also said: the meaning is "let each of you come to the other in the coming into being of what is intended to be produced from you both." This was supported by the recitation of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid: "a'tiya" (come) and "qalata a'tayna" (they both said: we come), in that this is from al-mu'atah (mutual accord), meaning agreement. Al-Jawhari said: you say "atayt-hu 'ala dhalika al-amr mu'ataatan" (I came to him concerning that matter in accord) if you agree with him and obey him, because two parties in agreement come to each other. He took that to be a sent figurative expression (majaz mursal), its relation being necessity. Ibn Jinni said: it means hastening (al-musara'ah), and this is also good. Most of the eminent scholars did not take it to be from ityan (giving), because it is not clear. Ibn Atiyyah took it as from that and implied an object: "give from yourselves of obedience what I intended from you." What came earlier is better, and what we previously mentioned in the first of the aspects of the speech comes similarly here, as is not hidden.

People have differed regarding the matter of precedence and delay in the creation of each of the heavens and what is in them, and the earth and what is in it. This is due to the verses and hadiths whose apparent meaning is contradictory. Some went to the precedence of the creation of the earth, based on the apparent meaning of this verse, where in it He first mentioned the creation of the earth, the placing of the mountains in it, and the measuring of its sustenance. Then He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿Then He istawa (turned) to the heaven﴾ ... etc. He refused that the command of coming to the earth be a command of creation (amr takwin). They also relied on the apparent meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, in the verse of al-Baqarah (29): ﴿He it is who created for you all that is in the earth, then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾, and on the beginning of the verses of al-Nazi'at, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or the heaven which He built? He raised its height and made it level. He darkened its night and brought out its forenoon. And the earth after that He spread out. He brought forth from it its water and its pasture. And the mountains He set firm. As a provision for you and your cattle﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27–33]. This is because its apparent meaning indicates that the creation of the earth and what is in it of water, pasture and mountains came later. That is because "that" refers to what came before, which is the raising of the height and the leveling. The word "the earth" is in the accusative governed by an implied verb in the manner of exegetical interpretation (shart al-tafsir, a specific grammatical construction), meaning: "and He spread out the earth after raising the heaven and leveling it, He spread it..." etc. Others said: "the earth" is in the accusative governed by an implied verb like "remember" or "reflect," or "mention the earth after that," not by an implied verb in the manner of exegetical interpretation. Or it is governed by the verb and "after that" refers to what was previously mentioned, namely the mention of the creation of the heaven, not the creation of the heaven itself. This indicates that it comes later in mention than the creation of the heaven, as an alert that it was deficient in the first place. However, this is a completion, as when you say: "such and such," and then you say "after that" (ba'da dhalika) "so and so." This is common in the usage of Arabs and non-Arabs. It seems that "after that" in this sense is the reverse when it is used for a later rank and for magnification. "Thumma" (then) is also used in this sense, and so is "fa" (then).

Some go, regarding the answer, to what Ibn Abbas said. For al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related with a sound chain of narration from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: A man came to Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, and said: "I see things in the Qur'an that conflict for me." He said: "Bring what conflicts for you of that." He said: "I hear God Exalted saying: ﴿Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth...﴾ up to ﴿willingly﴾, so He begins with the creation of the earth in this verse before the creation of the heaven. Then He, Glorified is He, said in the other verse: ﴿Or the heaven, He built it...﴾ then He said: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾. So He, Majestic is His affair, begins with the creation of the heaven before the creation of the earth." Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: "As for the creation of the earth in two days, the earth was created before the heaven, and the heaven was smoke, so He leveled them as seven heavens in two days after the creation of the earth. As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾, He says: He placed in it a mountain, placed in it a river, placed in it trees, and placed in it seas." End of quotation.

Al-Khafaji said: He means that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He brought forth from it its water﴾ is a substitute or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) for "spread it out," in the sense of "spread it," clarifying what is meant by it. Thus its delay in this verse is not in the sense of the delay of its essence, but in the sense of the delay of the creation of what is in it, its completion, and its arrangement, indeed the creation of enjoyment and benefit from it. For the remoteness (al-ba'idah) may be in terms of the thing itself, and it may be in terms of its last part and its specified condition, as when you say: "I sent to you a messenger, then I had sent so-and-so to see what he would reach." The sending of the second came earlier, but what it was sent for comes later than it. So he made himself later. If you say: how is this with what Ibn Jarir and others related and authenticated from Ibn Abbas also, that "the Jews came to the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and asked him about the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'God Exalted created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and created the mountains and what is in them of benefits on Tuesday, and on Wednesday created the trees, water, cities, population and ruin. These are four. Then God Exalted said: ﴿Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance, in four days, equally, for those who ask﴾. And on Thursday He created the heaven, and on Friday He created the stars, the sun, the moon and the angels'" — this contradicts the first, because it requires that the creation of what is in the earth of trees, rivers and the like came before the creation of the heaven? I say: the apparent meaning is to interpret it as meaning that He created in what was mentioned the substance of that and its roots, since it is not conceivable that population and ruin came before the creation of the heaven. So its coordination with it is evidence of this, and there is no contradiction between the two hadiths, just as there is no disagreement among the verses. End of al-Khafaji's words.

It is not hidden that the statement of Ibn Abbas mentioned earlier is explicit that placing the mountains in the earth came after the creation of the heaven, and this is the apparent meaning of the verse of al-Nazi'at, if His saying "after that" is taken as relevant to His saying: ﴿And the mountains He set firm﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 32]. And the verse of Ha Mim al-Sajdah is apparent that the placing of the mountains was before the creation of the heavens. Then the narration of Ibn Jarir mentioned from him contradicts the report of Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, took my hand and said: God Exalted created the dust on Saturday, created the mountains in it on Sunday, created the tree on Monday, created the disliked things on Tuesday, created the light on Wednesday, spread the animals in it on Thursday, and created Adam after the afternoon prayer on Friday, at the last of creation, in the last hour of the day, between the afternoon prayer and the night."

In Sharh al-Muhadhdhab (Commentary on al-Muhadhdhab), this report was used as evidence that Saturday is the first day of the week rather than Sunday. He transmitted this from his Shafi'i companions and al-Asnawi and Ibn Asakir authenticated it. Al-Allamah Ibn Hajar said: this is what most scholars hold, and it is our school's position, meaning the Shafi'is, as in al-Rawdah and its origin. Indeed al-Suhayli in his Rawd (al-Rawd al-Unuf) said that no one said that the first day is Sunday except Ibn Jarir. Al-Nawawi, in one place, followed what implies that the first day is Sunday, and said: "On Monday, it was named thus because it is the second of the days." It was answered that he followed in the explanation of the naming, relying on the slightest connection on the weak opinion.

Al-Qaffal of the Shafi'is defended the first [report] by saying that the mentioned report is transmitted by Muslim alone, and the hadith scholars spoke against it, [citing] Ibn al-Madini, al-Bukhari and others, and they made it a statement of Ka'b, and that Abu Hurayrah only heard it from him, but it became confused for some of the narrators, so he made it marfu' (traced to the Prophet). It was answered that whoever preserved the raising (rafe') is a proof against whoever did not preserve it, and a trustworthy narrator's hadith is not rejected merely on the basis of conjecture. For this reason Muslim turned away from what those [scholars] said, relied on the marfu' version, and included its chain in his Sahih, so accepting it is obligatory.

Ahmad ibn Ahmad al-Muqri al-Maliki mentioned that Imam Ahmad also related it in his Musnad from Abu Hurayrah, marfu', with the wording: "Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ) interlaced his fingers with mine and said: 'Allah the Exalted created the earth on Saturday...'" [to the end of the hadith]. In al-Durr al-Manthur there are several reports from Ibn Abbas stating that the beginning of the creation of the earth was on Sunday. In it also, Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, tell us what Allah the Exalted created of creation in these six days.' He said: 'Allah the Exalted created the earth on Sunday and Monday, created the mountains on Tuesday, created the cities, the provisions, the rivers, their cultivation and their ruin on Wednesday, and created the heavens and the angels on Thursday, until three hours [remained] of Friday, and in the first hour of it He created the appointed terms, in the second the calamity, and in the third Adam.' They said: 'You have spoken truly, if you complete it.' The Prophet (ﷺ) understood what they intended, so he became angry, and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And We did not touch us with weariness﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾."

The Jews as a whole agree that the first day of the week is Sunday, citing what they call the Torah, and its apparent derivation requires this.

Whoever holds that the first [day] is Saturday says: there is no proof in that, because the naming was not established by a command from Allah the Exalted nor from His Messenger (ﷺ). Perhaps the Jews set the names of the week according to what they believe, and the Arabs took them from them. The only [names] mentioned in the Qur'an are al-Jumu'ah and al-Sabt, and these are not from the numerals. Moreover, even if this naming were established from the Arabs, it would not be a proof, because the Arabs call the fifth of a group rub' and its ninth 'ushr. This is the very thing from which Ibn Abbas derived his statement, which he almost stood alone in, that the day of 'Ashura' is the ninth day of Muharram and Tasu'a' is its eighth day. It is not hidden that the first answer is outside fairness, for the Arabs have other names for the days of the week, among which are some that indicate this as well, namely: awwal, ahwan, jubar, dubar, mu'nis, 'arubah and shiyar. It is not fitting for a fair person to think that the Arabs followed the Jews in this and Islam came and confirmed them in it. I wonder: if those names were a following of the Jews, then what are the correct names which the originator of the language of the Arabs set, not following the Jews in them? The second answer is very far from the apparent [meaning].

Al-Wahidi in al-Basit transmitted from Muqatil that the creation of the heavens precedes the bringing into being of the earth, let alone its spreading out, and al-Imam chose this, and some attributed it to the verifying exegetes. They interpreted the verse by saying that creation is not an expression for bringing into existence and origination, but rather an expression for decree (taqdir). Its meaning with respect to Him the Exalted is His judgment that it will come to be, and His decree of the Mighty and Majestic with that, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. On this view there must be an interpretation of (made and blessed), similar to what I heard about al-Irshad. It was also permitted that khalaqa and what follows it remain as they naturally appear, and the speech be taken as referring to the will to will, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿When you rise to prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], i.e., by Him who willed the creation of the earth in two days and willed to place firm mountains in it.

They said: thumma (then) indicates a difference in rank, which is treated as temporal delay, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]. The subject of kana is a pronoun referring to the doer of ﴿he did not attempt the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11], namely the disbelieving human. And His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿freeing a neck﴾ ﴿or feeding on a day of severe hunger﴾ ﴿an orphan near of kin﴾ ﴿or a needy person in misery﴾ [al-Balad: 13–16] is an explanation of "the steep path." The apparent order would require placing faith before it, but thumma here is for delay in rank, metaphorically. In al-Kashf it is stated that what al-Wahidi transmitted is free of difficulty, and that thumma is definitely [to be read as] delay in rank in this surah and in al-Sajdah, and this is more in accord with the well-known principles of the philosophers. But it does not agree with what has come that the beginning was on Sunday, and the creation of the heavens and what is in them was on Thursday and Friday, and at the end of Friday Adam (peace be upon him) was completed. In al-Bahr, what we say is: the disbelievers were rebuked and reproached for their disbelief in the One from whom all these things came, without temporal order; and thumma is for the order of reports, not the order of time and interval. As if He, glory be to Him, said: by the One who informed you that He created the earth and placed in it firm mountains, blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance, then informed you that He rose over the heaven. So there is no indication in the verse of temporal order in the sequence of occurrence. And since the creation of the heaven is more wondrous in power than the creation of the earth, the reporting of it is resumed with thumma; so it is for the order of reports, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ after His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿he did not attempt the steep path﴾, and His saying the Exalted: ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 154] after His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾ [al-An'am: 151]. And His saying, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿So He said to them and to the earth﴾ is after His informing, the Exalted, of what He informed, as a depiction of their creation in accordance with His will, the Exalted, like your saying: "Have you seen the one I praised, when I said to him, 'You are a knowledgeable, righteous man'?" This is a depiction of what you praised him with and an explanation of it. Likewise, He, glory be to Him, informed that He created such-and-such, and He brought that into being in a way that did not deviate from His will. End. The apparent meaning of what he mentioned regarding His saying the Exalted: ﴿So He said to it﴾ ... etc. is that the saying is after the bringing into being. Some eminent scholars said that it is permissible that this be for illustration or imagery, to indicate that the heavens and the earth are places where His power, the Exalted, acts as He wills, in bringing into being and perfecting, in essence and attribute; and it serves as a preface to His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿so He completed them﴾, i.e., since creation was by this ease, He completed the heavens and perfected their creation in two days. Thus this statement is valid before their existence and after it, and during it, since the purpose is not to indicate occurrence.

It was mentioned, regarding the wisdom of placing the creation of the earth and what is in it first in mention here and in Surah al-Baqarah, before the creation of the heavens, and the reverse in Surah al-Nazi'at, that it may be that in the first two the context is one of favour and enumerating blessings, so its requirement is to mention first what is nearest of the blessings to the addressees; and the context in the third is one of showing the perfection of power, so its requirement is to mention first what is more indicative of its perfection. It is related from al-Hasan that He, the Exalted, created the earth at the site of Bayt al-Maqdis like a grinding stone, with smoke clinging to it; then He raised the smoke, created the heavens from it, held the stone in its place, and spread the earth out from it. This is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Did not those who disbelieved see that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, then We parted them?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30], and so on.

Some scholars took this as evidence that the spreading (dahw) of the earth was delayed after the creation of the heaven. But in al-Irshad it is stated that it is not explicit in that, for the spreading of
