al-Ard (the earth) is coordinated by the conjunction *wa* (and) with the clause about the rising of the smoke and the creation of the heaven. Therefore there is no indication of sequence in that, decisively. In *al-Kashshaf* (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari) it is stated that it indicates that the heaven being smoke precedes the spreading out (*dahw*) of the earth and its leveling. Rather, the apparent meaning of His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke﴾ indicates this. The bringing into being of the luminous jewel, and looking upon it with the eye of majesty, underlaid with mercy and beauty; its being spread out; the separation of its subtle part from its dense part; the rising of the subtle smoky substance and the remaining of the dense: all of this precedes the six days, and it is established in a sound report, and it does not contradict the verses.

Some scholars chose that the creation of the remote substance of the heavens and the earth was at one time, and it is the luminous jewel or other than it. Likewise the separation of the substance of each from the other and their distinction from one another, I mean the *fatq* (rending apart), and the bringing out of the subtle parts, which is the near substance of the heavens, and the retaining of the dense, which is the near substance of the earth. For the separation of the subtle from the dense necessitates the separation of the dense from it, and vice versa. As for the creation of each in the form in which it is witnessed, it was not at one time. Rather, the creation of the heavens precedes the creation of the earth in time. No one should doubt the delay of the creation of the earth with all that is in it after the creation of the heavens in this manner. And when it is permissible to read *thumma* (then) as indicating sequence in reporting, the matter of what is supposed to be a contradiction among the verses and reports becomes easy. This, and Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

One of the later scholars has a strange discourse on the verse, by which he removed what is supposed to be a conflict between the verses indicating that the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them was in six days, such as His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-Furqan: 59; al-Sajdah: 4], and His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf: 38]. And this verse, from which it is imagined that the creation of those was in eight days. He said: a thing has a ruling from the standpoint of its essence and self, and a ruling from the standpoint of its attributes, its relations, its connections, its requirements, its completions, and all that is attributed to it. Each of these has a counted term and a limited boundary, which He, glorified is He, manifests in that by the times specific to it and the periods appointed for it, and these vary and differ. Allah, the Exalted, created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in their own essence in six days. This was at their coming into being in their essence, from His, glorified is He, creating them from the sea resulting from the melting of the red ruby, when He, may His majesty be exalted, looked upon it with the look of awe, so it surged until froth came forth from it and the smoke rose. He created the heaven from the smoke, the earth from the froth, the stars from the sparks hidden in the froth of the sea, and the fire, the air and the water from a body denser than the smoke and more subtle than the froth. The heaven is a singular reality in its essence and has the capacity for multiplicity and plurality according to the manifestation of its state in the knowledge of the unseen. So its determination into seven in a specific respect, and the placement of each heaven in its specific station, entails a specific ruling which requires a making other than its making in itself. This is what is called *qadar* (measure), and the determination of the limits, which is the constructive geometry. This making is a branch of the creating, and its like is other than its like, decisively, as His saying, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿And He created everything and determined it with precise measure﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]. It may also be called *taswiyah* (leveling) and *qada'* (decree), as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and leveled them as seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], and His, the Exalted, saying here: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke﴾ up to His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾. As for the measuring of the sustenance of the earth, the giving of blessing, and the generating of what is generated, these have counted days and limited boundaries, and they do not enter into the days of the creation of the heavens and the earth, because they are for the bringing into being of their own selves. So the four days mentioned in the verse are only for the placing of the firm mountains, the measuring of sustenance, and the producing of blessing, and they are not from those six. Likewise the two days for the leveling of the heaven and its completing as seven heavens are outside of them. So in the verse under discussion there is nothing except that the creation of the earth was in two days. As for the creation of the heavens and what lies between them and the earth, no period is mentioned for it in the verse. Rather, it mentions only the period of the completing of the heavens, which is other than their creation, and the period of placing the firm mountains, measuring the sustenance, and producing blessing. That is other than the creation of the earth and what is between it and the heaven. So there is no contradiction between it and the verses indicating that the creation of the heavens

[Page 109]

and the earth and what is between them was in six days. Nor is this disturbed by what is narrated from al-Sadiq, that Allah, glorified is He, created the earths on Sunday and Monday, created their sustenance on Tuesday, created the heavens on Wednesday and Thursday, and created their sustenance on Friday; and that is the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾. Because, after accepting its soundness, what is mentioned in it is that the sustenance was created in two days, not that it was measured. And between creating and measuring there is a vast difference. So the creation of sustenance is an expression for bringing into being its essential elements, its substances, its causes and its means; then when they exist they are measured and detailed according to the known stages. So there is no difficulty.

What is strange is that one who finds this matter problematic does not consider the meanings of the divine expressions according to the Qur'anic and linguistic rules, so he needed, in its resolution, to undertake the strained imposition of hidden matters and the adoption of unsatisfactory interpretations. Then this man mentioned for the word "day" more than sixty usages, one of which is the rank, and he transmitted this from his shaykh, and I saw it in some books by others. He allowed its intention in the verse, and likewise allowed the intention of other usages. He mentioned the secret of the creation of the heavens and the earth in six days and lengthened the discussion on this matter. This was within a treatise he composed when he was asked for an answer to what is supposed to be a contradiction, other than what they mentioned as an answer to that. Whoever reads that treatise hears from it a clatter without weapons, and feels a flight in the air of what he claims as verification without wings. How much in it is a statement without a support, and a claim whose proof he did not bring. So upon you is a thorough reflection on what the commentators mentioned and what this man mentioned, and do not be one who turns aside from fairness or accompanies partisanship. And Allah, the Exalted, is the Granter of success.

And what was previously mentioned about carrying His, the Exalted, saying ﴿They said: We come willingly﴾ as a figurative expression is what a group of commentators adopted. A group said: they both spoke with real speech, and Allah, the Exalted, gave them life and perception. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is the best, because nothing repels it, and the lesson in it is more complete and the power in it more evident. It is not hidden that the first meaning is more eloquent. Whoever holds that inanimate things have a perception suitable to them takes the apparent meaning of the verse, and perhaps it is one of his proofs for that. Some of them mentioned, regarding His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And He inspired in each heaven its command﴾, that He, glorified is He, specified each heaven with what distinguishes it from the other heaven of essential attributes, and made that a reason for using the plural for the heavens and the singular for the earth. Al-A'mash read *"aw kurhan"* with a *damma* on the *kaf*. Abu Hayyan said: the more correct view is that it is a dialect for compulsion upon something, and most hold that *al-kurh* with a *damma* means hardship.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 13:

﴿Then if they turn away﴾ is connected to His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Say: Do you indeed...﴾ etc. That is: if they turn away from reflecting upon the great matters mentioned that call to faith, or from faith after this clarification, ﴿then say﴾ to them: ﴿I have warned you﴾, that is, I warn you. The past tense form is used to indicate the certainty of the warning, which points to the certainty of what is warned against, ﴿of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿAd and Thamud﴾, that is, a punishment like their punishment. This was said by Qatadah. It is clear according to the view that ṣāʿiqah (thunderbolt) in the language can mean punishment. Some scholars rejected this and considered what was mentioned to be a metaphor, meaning a punishment of severe impact, as if it were a thunderbolt like their thunderbolt. In either case, the meaning is: I have informed you of the descent of a thunderbolt.

Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sulami and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿ṣaʿqatan mithla ṣaʿqati﴾ without alif in both places and with the ʿayn sukun (ṣaʿqah), which is the single instance of ṣaʿq (a striking down), or ṣaʿq. It is said: the thunderbolt struck him with a striking down (ṣaʿqan), so he was struck down (faṣaʿiqa ṣaʿqan) with a fatha, that is, he perished by the thunderbolt, the calamity befalling him.

[p. 110]

﴿When the messengers came to them﴾, i.e., came to ʿĀd and Thamūd. The use of the plural for two (*jamʿ* for *ithnayn*) is found here, and it is common. Likewise, *al-rusul* ("the messengers") is used in this way. It has been said that the word may include the messenger of a messenger. For the first (ʿĀd and Thamūd), it is also permissible that the plural refers to the individuals of the two tribes.

The grammarians gave several possibilities for the grammatical function of *idh* ("when"). The first is that it is an adverb of time governing *anzartukum* ("I have warned you"). The second is that it is an adjective (*ṣifah*) of the first *ṣāʿiqah* ("thunderbolt"). An objection to these two is that it would require the warning of the one (the Prophet, ﷺ) and the thunderbolt with which he warned to occur at the time when the messengers came to ʿĀd and Thamūd, and this is not the case. The third is that it is an adjective of the second *ṣāʿiqah*. This has been criticized on the grounds that it would require omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause (*ṣilah*), which is not permitted according to the Basrans, or else describing a definite noun with an indefinite one. The fourth, which Abū Ḥayyān preferred, is that it is an object (*maʿmūl*) of *ṣāʿiqat ʿĀd wa-Thamūd* ("the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd"), on the basis that the term here means the punishment; otherwise, in its known meaning, it is a body (a mass of destruction) to which an adverbial phrase cannot be attached. There is something in this that is not hidden. The fifth, which many preferred, is that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of the thunderbolt, because it is definite by virtue of the construct phrase (*iḍāfah*). Some permit it also to be a circumstantial clause of the first (thunderbolt), because it is specified by a description that is itself specified by the construct phrase. Thus the possibilities are six.

﴿From before them and from behind them﴾ is connected to *jāʾat-hum* ("came to them"). The pronoun added to it refers to ʿĀd and Thamūd. The two directions are a metonymy (*kināyah*, an expression in which the literal words stand for a broader meaning) for all directions, as is known in similar cases. That is, "the messengers came to them from all their directions." The coming to them from all directions means exerting full effort in calling them (to faith), by way of metonymy. It is also possible that what is "before them" means the past time, and what is "behind them" means the future, or the reverse. In this case the adverb of place is used metaphorically for time. The meaning is that they came to them with warning about what befell the disbelievers like them in the past, and with caution about what would overtake them in the Hereafter.

This was reported from al-Ḥasan. It is also permissible that the pronoun added to it refers to the messengers, meaning that "the messengers came to them", both the earlier and the later ones, by treating the coming of their words and their call to the truth as the coming of themselves. Hūd and Ṣāliḥ were calling them to faith in them and in all the messengers, including those who came before them and those who would come after them. So it is as if the messengers had come to them and addressed them with the words of God, ﴿that you worship none but God﴾. This explanation was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Farrāʾ held it.

Some eminent scholars stated that *min bayni aydīhim* ("from before them") here is a circumstantial clause of the messengers, not connected to *jāʾat-hum*. The plural of "messengers" is apparent under this reading. It has been said that the coming of the messengers from before them and from behind them may be a metonymy for abundance, as in God's words: ﴿Their provision comes to them abundantly from every place﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:112]. Al-Ṭabarī said: the pronoun in God's words ﴿from before them﴾ refers to ʿĀd and Thamūd, and in His words ﴿and from behind them﴾ it refers to the messengers. Abū Ḥayyān criticized this in *al-Baḥr*, saying that it departs from the apparent sense by separating the pronouns and obscuring the meaning, since the sense would become: "the messengers came to them from before them, and came to them from behind the messengers", that is, from behind themselves. This is a meaning that cannot be understood unless the pronoun in *min khalfihim* ("from behind them") refers verbally to the messengers while it refers in meaning to other messengers. Thus it is as if it was said: "the messengers came to them from before them and from behind other messengers." This is like the saying: "I have a dirham and its half", meaning "and half of another dirham." Its remoteness is not hidden.

Of the destroyed nations, ʿĀd and Thamūd were singled out for mention because the Quraysh knew their circumstances and because they had passed by their lands in Yemen and al-Ḥijr.

The word *an* (that) may be explanatory (*mufassirah*) of the coming of the messengers, since it is by revelation and by laws, and so it contains the meaning of speaking. *Lā* is then prohibitive ("do not"). It may also be the verbal particle *an* (that), with *lā* again prohibitive. The verbal *an* may be joined to a prohibition just as it is joined to a command, in a discussion known in its place. Al-Ḥawfī made *lā* a negation and *an* an accusative particle governing the verb. It has also been said that *an* is the light form of the heavy *inna* (*al-mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah*), with an implied pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*) accompanying it. An objection to this is that it only occurs after verbs of certainty, and that the predicate of the *an* construction cannot be a command except by interpretation. This may be answered by supposing a verb of saying, and by noting that the coming of messengers is like revelation in meaning, so it takes *an* after it just as revelation does, since it implies what conveys certainty, as al-Raḍī and others have indicated. The strain in this is not hidden, and it is unnecessary. On the assumption that *an* is either verbal or light, the sentence would be with a preposition implied, that is, *bi-an* ("that"): "that you worship none but God."

﴿They said: "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels."﴾ The object of the verb of willing is omitted. Al-Zamakhsharī supplied it as "sending of messengers", meaning "if our Lord had willed the sending of messengers." ﴿He would have sent down angels﴾, i.e., He would have sent them. But since their sending is by way of warning, it is said "He would have sent down" (*la-anzala*). Some said: the sending down of angels was not supplied, on the basis that it is customary to supply the object of the verb of willing after the conditional particle *law* from the content of the condition, because this would be empty of conveying what they meant, namely the denial that God sends humans. The customary practice is not consistently followed. Abū Ḥayyān said: the actual supplied phrase is "if our Lord had willed the sending down of angels bearing the message to mankind, He would have sent them down with it", and this is more forceful in rejecting the sending of humans, since they made it dependent on the sending down of angels, and He, glory be to Him, did not will that. How then would they will it for humans? This is a good interpretation.

﴿So we are, in what you have been sent with, disbelievers.﴾ That is, "in that which you have been sent with, according to your claim." This contains a mocking tone towards them. ﴿Disbelievers﴾, because you are humans like us, and you have no superiority over us. The *fa* (so) is the *fāʾ* of consequence and causation, so the sentence contains an implicit hint of an exceptive syllogism, meaning: "but He did not send down (angels)." It may also be a causal *fāʾ* explaining their conditional statement, meaning: "We only said that because we deny what you have been sent with, just as we deny your messengership." The *mā* (what), as we have indicated, is a relative pronoun. That it is a verbal *mā* and that the pronoun in *bihi* ("with it") refers to their statement ﴿that you worship none but God﴾ is against the apparent sense. Al-Bayhaqī in *al-Dalāʾil* and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: "Abū Jahl and the chiefs of Quraysh said: 'The matter of Muḥammad (ﷺ) has become confused for us. So if you were to seek out a man knowledgeable in magic, soothsaying and poetry, and he were to speak to him and then come back to us with a clarification of his affair.' ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah said: 'By God, I have heard poetry, soothsaying and magic, and I know something of that, and nothing of it is hidden from me. If it is as you say, I will go to him.' So he came to him and said: 'O Muḥammad, are you better, or Hāshim? Are you better, or ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib?' He gave him no answer. He said: 'Why do you revile our gods and mislead our fathers? If it is leadership you want, we will raise our banners for you. If it is wealth you want, we will gather for you from our wealth what will make you and your descendants after you rich. If it is marriage you want, we will marry you to ten women, choosing from whichever daughters of Quraysh you wish.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was silent and said nothing. When he had finished, he (ﷺ) said: 'In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. A Book whose verses are made distinct, an Arabic Qurʾan' — and he recited until he reached: ﴿But if they turn away, say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd.﴾" ʿUtbah put his hand over the mouth of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and begged him by the ties of kinship to stop. He returned to his family and did not go out to Quraysh. When he was delayed from them, Abū Jahl said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, I think ʿUtbah has only inclined towards Muḥammad (ﷺ) and has been impressed by his food. Nothing else would have done this except some need that has befallen him. Let us go to him.' They went to him, and Abū Jahl said: 'By God, O ʿUtbah, we only suppose that you have inclined towards Muḥammad and that his affair has impressed you. If you have a need, we will gather for you from our wealth what will make you independent of Muḥammad (ﷺ).' He became angry and swore by God, exalted is He, that he would never speak to Muḥammad (ﷺ) again. He said: 'You know that I am the wealthiest of Quraysh. But I went to him, and he related to them the story. He answered me with something which, by God, is neither magic, nor poetry, nor soothsaying. He recited: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. A Book whose verses are made distinct, an Arabic Qurʾan, until ﴿I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd.﴾ I put my hand over his mouth and begged him by the ties of kinship, and he stopped. You know that Muḥammad (ﷺ), when he says something, does not lie, and I feared that the punishment would descend upon you.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 15:

﴿As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant in the land without right﴾. This begins the detailing of what each of the two groups had in terms of wrongdoing and punishment. Because the detail branches out from the summary, it is joined with the fa' of causality (fa' al-sababiyyah). The account of ʿĀd is mentioned first because they are older in time. That is: ﴿as for ʿĀd, they magnified themselves in the land﴾ where magnifying oneself is not fitting for its people, ﴿without right﴾, meaning without deserving to be magnified.

Page 112
It has also been said: they magnified themselves against obeying the command of Allah, mighty and majestic, and against accepting what the messengers brought them. ﴿And they said﴾, deceived by their strength: ﴿Who is stronger than us in strength?﴾ That is, there is no one stronger than us in strength. The interrogative is a denial. This explains their claim to deserve greatness and is their answer to the messengers concerning the punishment with which the messengers warned them. They were people of tall bodies and great stature, and their strength reached the point that a man would pull a rock from a mountain and lift it with his hand.

﴿Did they not see﴾, meaning they were heedless and did not reflect, or did not know with a clear knowledge resembling direct witness and observation, ﴿that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength﴾, in power. He, exalted is He, is capable in Himself, empowered over what is endless, strong over what none other can do, mighty and majestic, the bestower of strength and power upon every strong and capable one. In this there is an indication that what the messengers warned them of did not come from their own selves based on strength they possessed, but was from Allah, exalted, the creator of strengths and powers, while they knew that He, mighty and majestic, is stronger than them. The interpretation of strength as power is because it is one of its meanings, as the words of al-Raghib indicate.

Some have claimed that strength is an accident from which Allah, exalted, is exempt, but it entails power, so it was expressed by it through metonymic correspondence (mushakalah). The phrase ﴿who created them﴾ was placed in the relative clause rather than "the creation of the heavens and the earth," because of their claim of intensity in strength, and in this there is a kind of mockery of them. ﴿And they used to deny Our signs﴾, meaning they would reject them while knowing their truth. This is a conjunction with ﴿they were arrogant﴾ or ﴿they said﴾, so the clause ﴿Did they not see﴾ … etc., together with what it is conjoined to, is a parenthetical insertion. It is also permitted that it alone be a parenthetical insertion, with the waw being parenthetical rather than conjunctive.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 16:**

﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind﴾. Mujahid said: "It is intensely hot, so it derives from *ṣarr* with a fatha on the *ṣād*, meaning heat." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: "It is cold, destroying by its severe coldness. It derives from *ṣirr* with a kasra on the *ṣād*, which is the cold that *yuṣirru* (gathers and contracts) the outer skin of a person and constricts it." The first meaning is more suitable to the lands of the Arabs. Al-Suddi, Abu 'Ubaydah, Ibn Qutaybah, al-Tabari and a group (of scholars) also said: "It is resounding, from *ṣarra yaṣirru* when it makes a sound." Ibn al-Sikkit said: "*Ṣarṣar* may be from *al-ṣarra*, which is the cry, and from it is [the verse] ﴿Then his wife came forward in a cry﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 29]." In a hadith: "God, exalted is He, commanded the keepers of the wind, and they opened on them an opening the size of a ring's hoop. Had they opened it the size of an ox's nostril, the world would have been destroyed." It is also narrated that the wind used to carry the caravan with its loads and throw them into the sea.

﴿In days of ill omen﴾. *Nahisat* is the plural of *nahisah* with a kasra on the *ḥā'*, an adjective of the pattern *ṣifah mushabbahah* (the resemblance-adjective form) from *naḥisa yanḥasu niḥsan*, like *ʿalima ʿilman*, the opposite of *saʿida saʿdan*.

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), Abu 'Amr, al-Nakha'i, 'Isa and al-A'raj read *nuḥusāt* with a sukun on the *ḥā'*. This may be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) described by it for emphasis (*mubalaghah*), or it may be an adjective lightened from the pattern *faʿila*, like *ṣaʿiba*. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), I searched what the grammarians of morphology (al-taṣrīfiyyūn) mentioned of adjectives coming from the intransitive *faʿila* pattern, and they mentioned no instance with a sukun on the middle letter; they mentioned only verbs with a kasra, like *faraḥa*, and the adjective patterns *afʿal* like *aḥwar*, *faʿlān* like *shabʿān*, and *fāʿil* like *sālim*. The word is an adjective of *ayyām* (days). It is pluralised with the *alif* and *tā'* because it describes what is not rational. The intended meaning is that they were days of ill omen for them, since they were punished in them. The same day may be described as ill-omened or auspicious in relation to two different persons: it is called auspicious in relation to one who is made to enjoy blessings on it, and it is called ill-omened in relation to one who is punished on it. This is not one of the particular properties of times that people imagine. Al-Karmani in his *Manasik* reports from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "All days belong to God, exalted is He, but He created some of them as ill-omened and some as auspicious." The interpretation of *naḥisāt* as *mashā'īm* (ill-omened) is related from Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. Al-Dahhak said: "That is, extremely cold, so that the cold was a punishment for them." Al-Asma'i recited, using *naḥs* in the sense of cold:

*"As if its pure wine were mixed with naḥs (cold)"*

It was also said: "*Naḥisāt* means days with dust." Al-Jubba'i took this view, and from it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*"He set out before the rising of the sun / for the hunt, on a day of little naḥs (dust)"*

He means: little dust. These days were, according to some reports, from the end of Shubat, and they are called "the days of the old woman." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah that they were the last of Shawwal, from Wednesday to Wednesday. It is also reported that no people were punished except on a Wednesday. Al-Suddi said: "The first of them was the morning of Sunday." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "Friday."

﴿That We may make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾. The punishment is attributed to *khizy* (disgrace), which is humiliation, with the intention of describing the punishment by it, as in the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing﴾. *Khizy* is originally an attribute of the one who is punished, but it is applied to the punishment by a metonymical attribution (*isnad majazi*) for emphasis. This indicates that the humiliation of the disbeliever increased until his punishment came to be described by it, as established in the saying "a poem that is poetic" (*shi'run sha'ir*). This is in contrast to their arrogance and self-magnification.

It was also read as *li-tudhīqahum* with a *tā'*, so that the agent is the pronoun referring to the wind or to the ill-omened days.

﴿And they will not be helped﴾, meaning, they will not be helped to avert the punishment from them in any way.

[Page 114]

﴿As for Thamud, We guided them﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: that is, We made it clear to them. According to what has been said, they meant by this the showing of the two paths of error and right guidance, as in His saying, ﴿And We showed him the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. This is more fitting with His saying, ﴿So they preferred blindness over guidance﴾, that is, they chose misguidance over guidance. The apparent meaning is that the two paths were made clear to them and they chose one of them. Ibn Zayd stated this explicitly; it is reported from him that he said: that is, We informed them of the guidance from misguidance. Many others interpreted the guidance here as indication (dalalah), that is, We pointed them to the truth by setting up proofs and sending messengers, and then they chose error. They did not interpret it as the guidance that leads to its goal (al-dalalah al-mawassilah), because of the apparent conflict with ﴿they preferred﴾ and what follows it.

The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that holds human beings act by independent choice) used this verse to argue that faith is by the servant's own independent choice, on the basis that His saying, ﴿We guided them﴾, indicates the setting up of evidences and the removal of excuse, and His saying, ﴿they preferred blindness﴾ and so on, indicates that they themselves preferred blindness. The answer, as given in al-Kashf, is that the word "preference" (al-istihbab) implies that the power of God, exalted is He, is the effective cause, and that the servant's power has some involvement, since love is by agreement not something chosen, whereas preferring blindness out of love, which is what istihbab is, belongs to the realm of choice. So look at this subtle point and you will see a wondrous marvel. The Imam, the caller to God, may God sanctify his secret, pointed to something similar. The meaning of love not being a matter of choice is that after the occurrence of the things on which it depends, which are matters of choice, it comes about through the pull of nature, without the person choosing the inclination of his heart and the attachment of his desire to the one he loves. So it is in itself not chosen, but in terms of its preconditions it is chosen. For this reason we are commanded to love God and His Messenger (ﷺ). In Tawq al-Hamamah by Ibn Saʿid, love is a natural spiritual inclination, and to this His saying, mighty and majestic is He, points: ﴿And He made from it its mate that he might find rest in her﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 189], that is, he inclines toward her. So He made the cause of her inclination that she is from him. This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Souls are armies gathered together." Love may also be for other things, such as beauty, kindness and perfection, and it has effects that are also called love, such as obedience and reverence. These are the things for which a person is held accountable, because they are matters of choice, so understand this.

Ibn Wththab, al-Aʿmash and Bakr ibn Habib read "wa-amma Thamudu" with a nominative ending and with tanwin (nunation, i.e., they read it as a declinable noun).

Al-Aʿmash and Ibn Wththab read it declined (ṣarf) throughout the Qur'an, except in His saying, ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel﴾ [al-Isra': 59], because in the Mushaf it is written without an alif. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Hurmuz, in one of the reports from him, and al-Mufaddal read it with the accusative and tanwin. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: al-Aʿmash, ʿAsim, and it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, "Thamudan" with the accusative and tanwin. Al-Mufaddal related from ʿAsim both readings. Non-declension (man al-ṣarf) is due to being a proper name and feminine, if the tribe is intended. Whoever declines it takes it as the name of a man. The accusative is by treating it as a case of supplementary verb (al-idmar ʿala shart al-tafsir), where the governing verb after it is understood, because "amma" is generally followed only by a noun.

It was also read with a damma on the thaʾ, as the plural of thamad, which is a small amount of water. They were named thus because they lived in the sands between Hadramawt and Sanaʿa, and they had little water.

﴿So the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them﴾. That is, the humiliation. It is an attribute of the punishment or a substitute for it. Describing it with it as a verbal noun is for emphasis. Likewise the annexation of "thunderbolt" to "punishment" indicates that their punishment is in fact humiliation, and that it has a thunderbolt. The thunderbolt means the fire that comes out of the clouds, as is well known. The customary cause of its occurrence is well known in the books of ancient philosophy. Those of modern philosophy, widely current today in the lands of the Romans and nearby places, have discussed this, saying in explanation of how the thunderbolt bursts forth: It is known that the release of the electricity in the clouds, which is a particular force in bodies similar to the force of electricity by which straw and the like are drawn toward it, happens only through the union of the electricity of bodies with one another. So when the cloud approaches the earthly bodies, the cloud's electricity seeks to unite with the earth's electricity, and an electric spark bursts between them, striking the earthly bodies. The strength of the thunderbolt varies according to the variation of the vaporous transformation, so it is not the same in all lands and seasons. They explained this at length; whoever wishes it should return to their books. It has also been said: the thunderbolt here means the cry (al-sayha), as it is mentioned in other verses. There is no barrier to combining the two.

Ibn Muqsim read "al-hawan" with a fatha on the ha and an alif after the waw. ﴿Because of what they were earning﴾, that is, from choosing error over guidance. This is an explicit statement of what the particle "fa" (so) implies.

﴿And We saved﴾ from that thunderbolt ﴿those who believed and used to fear Allah﴾ because of their faith and their persistence in taqwā (God-consciousness, piety). What is meant by it is the taqwā of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said: the taqwā of the thunderbolt. And one who guards against the punishment of God, Exalted is He, is one who is mindful of God, Glorified is He, but this is not the case.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 41, verse 19:

﴿And on the Day when the enemies of God are gathered to the Fire﴾. This begins the explanation of their deferred punishments, after mention of their punishments in this world. Describing them as "the enemies of God, exalted is He" serves to censure them and to indicate the reason for the various torments that befall them. It has been said that the intended meaning is the disbelievers of the first and last generations.

This has been objected to on the grounds that His later words, ﴿among nations that passed away before them, of jinn and humankind﴾ [Fussilat: 25], are nearly explicit that the intended meaning is the specific disbelievers already known. As for His words ﴿to the Fire﴾, it has been said that the intended meaning is "to the place of reckoning." Expressing it as "the Fire" indicates that the Fire is the outcome of their gathering and that they are on the verge of entering it. There is no obstacle to keeping it on its apparent meaning, and to the view that the testimony is multiple: their limbs testify against them at the place of standing once, and at the brink of Hell another time.

﴿And on the Day﴾ may be governed by an implied verb "remember," which is coordinated with His words ﴿So say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt﴾ [Fussilat: 13]. Or it may be an adverbial complement of an implied, delayed verb that has been omitted to suggest that expression falls short of detailing it. It has also been said that it is an adverbial complement of what His words ﴿so they are held back﴾ indicate, meaning that the first of them is held back until the last of them, so that they catch up with one another. This is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for their great number. It has also been said that they are driven and pushed into the Fire, and the *fa* in ﴿so they are held back﴾ is explanatory (*tafsiliyya*).

Zayd ibn 'Ali, Nafi', al-A'raj, and the people of Madina read *nahshuru* with the letter *nun*, and *a'da'* with the accusative case. Al-A'raj vowelled the *shin* with a kasra. It has also been read *yahshuru* in the active voice, with its subject being God, exalted is He, and *a'da'a Allah* in the accusative.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 20:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Until, when they come to it﴾, meaning the Fire, all of them, is the *ghayah* (end point) for ﴿they will be gathered﴾ or ﴿they will be driven on﴾. That is, ﴿until, when they are present at it﴾. The *ma* here is *mazidah* (an additional particle, *ziyadah*) to emphasise the connection of the testimony with the presence, because it emphasises what comes after it. So it emphasises the meaning of *idha* (when). *Idha* indicates the connection of the response (*jawab*) with the condition (*shart*), since both occur at one time. This is something unrelated to grammar, so there is no harm in the fact that the grammarians did not mention it, as Abu Hayyan censured and insisted, because they deny it.

There is an ellipsis (*hadhf*) in the speech, and the implied supposition (*taqdir*) is: ﴿until, when they come to it, and they are questioned about what they committed, and they deny it﴾. ﴿Their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ (Q 41:20). He dispensed with the omitted part by mentioning the testimony, since the testimony necessarily implies it. The supposition does not prevent the emphasis of the connection, since it suffices for the connection that these things happen in one session.

The apparent meaning is that the skins (*julud*) are the well-known ones. It was said that they are the limbs (*jawarih*), with the skins used as a metonymy for them. It was also said that they are a metonymy for the private parts. It was said: most of the exegetes, among them Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, hold this view. In al-Irshad it is said that this is the most suitable reading, given the specification of the question in

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 21:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾. For what the skins testify to of fornication is a greater crime and more repugnant, and more conducive to disgrace and punishment, than what the hearing and the sights testify to of the offences acquired through them. But there is room for objection here, and it is likely that the apparent meaning is preferable. It is also possible that the question was specifically directed to the skins because they are in plain view of them, unlike hearing and sight, or because the skins are what perceive the punishment through the power deposited in them, as his saying, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so that they may taste the punishment﴾ (al-Nisa': 56). Al-Jalabi said: then he related from al-Allama al-Thani concerning this that testimony from the skins is more wondrous and more remote, since it is not the nature of skins to perceive, unlike hearing and sight. He followed this with his words: "There is room for objection here, for the skin is the seat of the sense of touch, which is the most important of the senses for the living being, just as hearing and sight are the seats of hearing and seeing. And it is He who makes the entities speak, not the accidents. Moreover, touch encompasses taste, which is the most important after touch." Then he said: "There appears, in light of what we have established, another aspect of specification: the importance to the human being, and the encompassing of what is more important than others, is suitable to be a specifying factor. Thus the reversal of what they hoped for from its most perfect benefit is more wondrous, and such a one deserves rebuke more than others." It was objected to him that his rejoinder to al-Allama does not hit its target, since what he mentioned, that it is not the nature of skins to perceive, is not intended except as the perception of kinds of disobedience for which one is testified against, such as disbelief, lying, killing and fornication, for example, and the perception of such things is confined to hearing and sight.

You know, after setting aside the core of the discussion in this answer, that what al-Allama mentioned does not fit the apparent sense of the question, namely ﴿Why did you testify against us?﴾. The best of what has been said among the aspects of specification is: the defence of the skins is greater than the defence of hearing and sight, for if the skin of a single person were divided into parts, it would exceed a thousand hearings and sights, and it defends each part and fears that what would disgrace it might befall it. So testimony from the skins against them was more wondrous and more remote from occurring.

In a hadith: "The first part of a person to speak will be his left thigh, then the limbs will speak, and he will say: 'Woe to you! It was on your behalf that I was defending.'" As for the singular form of "hearing", its reason has already been mentioned at the beginning of the commentary. As for the reason for confining the mention to hearing, sight and skin, Abu Hayyan pointed to it, saying: "Since the senses are five, hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch, and taste is subsumed under touch, for the taste of what is tasted is perceived by the contact of the moist tongue's skin with it, and since the sense of smell carries no obligation, neither command nor prohibition, and it is weak, [the verse] confines itself among the senses to hearing, sight and touch." There is room for discussion in this. It seems to me that you will prefer that what is meant by the skins is other than hearing and the sights, and that the mention of hearing is because it is the means of perceiving most of the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanziliyya), and the mention of sights is because they are the means of perceiving most of the cosmic signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyya).

Each has been indicated in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them﴾ (Fussilat: 17) in one respect, and that their testimony concerns what relates to disbelief: hearing will testify against them that they denied the revealed signs which the messengers brought and which they heard from them, and sight will testify that they paid no heed to the cosmic signs which they saw, and disbelieved in what they indicate. Perhaps the testimony of the skins concerns what is other than disbelief among the acts of disobedience which the messengers, peace be upon them, forbade, such as fornication, for example. It is also permitted that the testimony of hearing is by perceiving the revealed signs, that of sight by perceiving the cosmic signs, and that of the skins concerns disbelief according to what each requires, and the other concerns acts of disobedience. There is no remoteness in including in "what they used to do" the perceiving of the signs and the sensing of them in both their kinds. So reflect.

Perhaps His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Why did you testify﴾ is a question about the causative reason. The plural form for rational beings in ﴿you testified﴾ and what follows is used even though its referent is not rational, because it occurs in the position of a question and answer which are specific to rational beings. Zayd ibn Ali read "Why did you testify" (limâ shahidtunna) with the feminine plural pronoun. ﴿They will say, "God, who made everything speak, has made us speak."﴾ That is, God, may He be exalted, made us speak and enabled us to clarify the reality, so we testify against you to what you did of the abominations, and we did not conceal anything. Since the meaning of the question is "for what causative reason did you testify?", what has been mentioned suits as an answer to it. It has been said: there is no intent at all here for a question; rather the intent is to express wonder from the outset, because wonder occurs regarding what its cause and reason are not known. So the question about the reason, which entails not knowing it, is made a metaphor or a metonymy for wonder. It has been said: when the cause becomes apparent, wonder ceases; as if it were said: our speech is not a wonder from the power of God, the Exalted, who made everything speak. In any case, the speaking is in its true meaning, as is apparent, and so is the testifying. It should not be said: the witnesses are themselves, and the hearing, sight and skins are instruments like the tongue, so what is the meaning of ﴿you testified against us﴾? For it is said: what is meant is not this kind of speech which is attributed in truth to the whole person, with the other being an instrument without power and will of its own, such that if it were attributed to it, it would be metaphorical, like the attribution of writing to the pen. Rather it is speech attributed in truth to the member, so that the member itself speaks by a power and will which God, the Exalted, created in it, just as a person speaks by means of an instrument. And how could it not be so, when their selves are averse to that and deny it? It has been said: the speakers are themselves, by those organs, except that they cannot prevent those organs from being instruments; for this reason the testimony against them was attributed to them. This is not worth anything. Some of them permitted that speech be a metaphor for indication, so that what is meant by testimony is the appearance of marks on the members indicating what they were involved in during the world, by a change in their forms and the like, which God, the Exalted, inspires in whoever sees them, that they were involved in it in the world, since the veil is lifted in the Hereafter. But this is contrary to the apparent sense of the verses and the hadiths, and there is no reason for it. On the apparent reading, "everything" must be specified to every living being that speaks, for not everything, nor every living being, speaks with true speech. Such specification is common, and among its instances is what has been said regarding ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾ (al-Baqara: 284; Al 'Imran: 29; al-Ma'ida: 19, 40; al-Tawba: 39) and ﴿It destroys everything﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 25). It is also permitted that the speaking in ﴿made us speak﴾ is in its true meaning, and the speaking in ﴿who made everything speak﴾ is taken as indication, so the general term remains general and does not need the specification mentioned. The expression of speech is then by way of a parallel (mushakala), but this is contrary to the apparent sense, and the relative clause, which implies causation, strongly rejects it. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He created you the first time, and to Him you will be returned﴾ may be part of the speech of the skins and the content of the saying; it may also be a new statement from His own speech, may He be exalted and glorified; the first is more apparent. In any case, the intended meaning is to confirm what precedes it: that the One able to create the first time is able to make speak. The form of the present tense is used, when the address is on the Day of Resurrection, even though the return there is established and not future, because what is meant by return is not merely the restoration to life by resurrection, but what includes it and what follows from it of everlasting punishment, which is anticipated at the time of address, with the expected being given precedence over the actual. It is also permitted that it is to bring the scene to mind, along with the observance of the rhyme (fawasil).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 22:

And His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And you did not conceal yourselves [from your sins] lest your hearing bear witness against you, nor your sight, nor your skins﴾. This is a report of what will be said to them on that Day from Him, exalted is He, by way of rebuke and reproach, confirming the answer of the skins. Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi) preferred the view that it is from the speech of the limbs. And ﴿lest it bear witness﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) with an omitted noun before it, meaning: you did not conceal yourselves in the world when committing the grave sins out of fear or aversion that your limbs would bear witness against you about that. That is, your concealment was not from fear of what was mentioned, nor from aversion to it. ﴿But you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do﴾. That is: but because of your thinking that Allah, exalted is He, does not know much of what you do, namely what you did in secret, so He will not make it manifest on the Day of Resurrection, and the limbs will not speak of it. Therefore you strove to conceal yourselves from creation but not from the Creator, mighty and majestic is He. Or it is with an omitted preposition attached to "you concealed yourselves." It is said: it is the preposition "bi" (with), and that from which one hides is the limbs, and the meaning is: you did not hide from them by way of "lest it bear witness against you," i.e., bear the testimony, since you did not think they would testify against you; rather you thought that Allah, glorified is He, does not know, so your concealment was not for this reason. It is also said: it is "min" (from), and the meaning is: it was not possible for you to conceal yourselves from the limbs, lest they bear the testimony against you when you commit what you commit; but you thought what you thought.

It is also said: "lest it bear witness" is an object of purpose, and that from which one conceals is the limbs, i.e., you did not conceal yourselves from your limbs out of fear that they would bear witness against you, but you thought... etc. It is also said: "you concealed yourselves" was made to imply the meaning of "thinking," so it took its construction, i.e., you did not conceal yourselves, thinking that the limbs would bear witness against you. This is supported by the words of Qatadah: meaning, you did not think that it would bear witness against you... etc. The truth is that this is an explanation of the resulting meaning.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and a group related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was concealed behind the curtains of the Ka'bah when three men came: a Qurashi and two Thaqafis, or a Thaqafi and two Qurashis, much fat on their bellies and little understanding in their hearts. They spoke words I did not hear. One of them said: Do you think Allah hears our speech? The other said: If we raise our voices, He hears it, and if we do not raise them, He does not hear. The other said: If He hears some of it, He hears all of it." He said: "I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah revealed: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing bear witness against you, nor your sight, nor your skins﴾ - to His saying, glorified is He - ﴿among the losers﴾." Thus the ruling reported then is specific to those who held that belief of disbelief, though it is rare among the disbelievers. In al-Irshad it is said: it is perhaps more fitting that "thinking" be taken in a metaphorical sense that encompasses its literal meaning and what is similar to it of actions that indicate it, as in His saying: ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾ [al-Humazah: 3], so that the reported state includes all kinds of disbelievers. So reflect.

In the verse there is an admonition that the believer should not pass through any state except with the awareness that over him is a watcher, as Abu Nuwas said:

When I am alone for a day, do not say "I was alone," but say: "Over me is a watcher."

And do not think that Allah is heedless for an hour,
nor that what is hidden from Him disappears.

[Page 118]

﴿And that﴾ refers to their assumption mentioned within His statement, glorified is He: ( you assumed ), together with the sense of distance it carries, to indicate the extreme remoteness of their rank in evil and wickedness. It is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), and His statement, exalted is He, ﴿your assumption which you assumed about your Lord﴾ is an apposition (badal, an appositive) to it. His statement, glorified is He, ﴿has ruined you﴾, meaning destroyed you, is the predicate (khabar). It is also permitted that ( your assumption ) be the predicate, or that ﴿has ruined you﴾ be a second predicate. Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that ( that ) refers to their earlier assumption, so the sense becomes "your assumption about your Lord, that He does not know your assumption about your Lord," and what is conveyed by the predicate is then what is conveyed by the subject, which is not permissible, like their saying: "The master of the slave-girl is her owner," and the grammarians have prohibited this. It has been answered that this does not necessarily follow from what was mentioned, since it is permissible to take the reference to be to a matter great in ugliness, so the concept varies with the variation of the designation, and the predication is valid, as in "this is Zayd." And even if it is granted that they are identical, the identity is like his saying:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry,"

which indicates perfection in beauty, as in this example, or in ugliness, as in the sentence under discussion. It has been said that the purpose of it is amazement and mockery. The predicate may also be used for something other than the predicate's usual benefit and its necessary implication. Some scholars chose, as the answer, what Ibn Hisham indicated in his commentary on:

"Su'ad has departed ....."

and he elaborated on it, that the benefit is obtained from the description and the qualifier of the predicate just as it is obtained from the predicate itself, like the circumstantial clause (hal, a circumstantial phrase). It is also permitted that the clause ﴿has ruined you﴾ be a circumstantial clause, with or without the particle qad. In all the possibilities, the relative clause ( ﴿your assumption﴾ ) is a qualifier. It has also been said that all three are predicates, so do not overlook this.

﴿So you became﴾ because of that evil assumption which destroyed you, ﴿among the losers﴾, since the faculties they were given for attaining happiness in this world and the Hereafter became [a cause of loss], because by them they sustain their life in this world and perceive what guides them to certainty and to knowledge of the Lord of the worlds, which leads to the happiness of the Hereafter. They became a cause of wretchedness in both abodes, since they led them to ingratitude for the blessings of the Provider, to disbelief in the Creator, to immersion in heedlessness, to committing sins, and to following desires.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 24:

﴿Then if they endure, the Fire is their abode﴾, meaning a place of lasting dwelling and residence for them, such that there is no escape from it for them. The consequent is ordered upon the condition because the presumption is that they endure, and the assumption is that patience benefits them, since it is the key to relief. Their patience will not benefit them if it does not reach its proper place, for the Fire is certainly their place. It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech and the sense is "or if they do not endure," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Endure it or do not endure it; it is the same for you﴾ [al-Tur: 16]. It has also been said that the meaning is "if they endure in abandoning your religion and following their desires, then the Fire is their abode," but this is not right. The shift (iltifat) is to indicate that their state warrants that He turn away from them and relate their bad condition to others, or to convey their removal from the realm of address and their being cast into the depths of the Fire's levels. ﴿And if they seek to be granted favour﴾, meaning they ask for al-'utba, which is returning to what they love, out of distress at their condition. ﴿Then they are not among those who are granted favour﴾, meaning those who are answered in it.

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning is, "If they make excuses, they are not among those who are excused."

Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Musa al-Aswari recited (qira'ah, a canonical or variant reading of the Qur'an) "wa in yusta'tabu" in the passive and "fa-ma hum mina al-mu'tibin" with the active participle (ism fa'il). The meaning is: if they are asked to satisfy their Lord, they will not do so, and that will not happen because they have departed from the world, the abode of deeds, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no one who can be granted favour (mustá'tab) after death." It is possible that this reading carries the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Had they been returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 25:

﴿And We appointed for them﴾ means We decreed. "And in al-Bahr" means We caused for them from where they did not reckon. It is said: We empowered and entrusted over them ﴿companions﴾, the plural of qarin, meaning close friends and associates from the misguided jinn. It is said: from among them and from mankind, who take control over them with the control of the qayd (the shell) over the egg. It is said: the root of qayd is substitution, and from it comes muqayadah (exchange) for mutual exchange. So the appointing of a companion to a person is either because he takes control of him, or because he takes him in exchange for another of his companions. ﴿And they made attractive to them﴾ means they made good and confirmed in their minds ﴿what was before them﴾. Ibn Abbas said: this is the matter of the Hereafter, since they told them that there is no Paradise, no Fire, and no Resurrection. ﴿And what was behind them﴾ is the matter of this world: misguidance, disbelief, and following desires. Al-Hasan said: what was before them is the matter of this world, and what was behind them is the matter of the Hereafter. Al-Kalbi said: what was before them is their deeds which they witness, and what was behind them is what they will do in the future. Every view has its direction, and perhaps the best is what is related from al-Hasan. ﴿And the word came into effect against them﴾ means it was established and confirmed against them: the word of punishment was fulfilled and its consequence and fulfillment realized. It is His saying to Iblis: ﴿So the truth is, and the truth I say: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together﴾ [Sad: 85]. It is a hal (circumstantial clause) from the genitive pronoun, meaning they are existing within a group of nations. It is said: "fi" here has the meaning of "ma'a" (with), and his saying admits both meanings:
