If you have been turned away from the best of deeds,
then among others too have they been turned away.

In al-Bahr, there is no need for tadmin (implicit meaning of a verb through another) given the soundness of the meaning of "fi". The indefiniteness of ﴿nations﴾ is for magnification, meaning among many nations. ﴿Who had passed away﴾ means who had gone by ﴿before them, of the jinn and mankind﴾ upon disbelief and disobedience, like the custom of these. ﴿Indeed they were losers﴾ is a causal clause explaining why they deserve punishment. The pronoun refers to them and to the nations, and it is permitted that it refers to them alone by the context.

And those who disbelieved said, (namely) the leaders of the polytheists to their followers, or some of them said to others: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾, meaning, do not pay attention to it. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ), when he was in Makkah, would raise his voice when reciting the Qur'an, and the polytheists would drive people away from him and say: 'Do not listen to this Qur'an.'" ﴿And make noise over it﴾, meaning, bring forth idle noise during its recitation so that the reciter is disturbed. By al-laghw (idle noise) is meant that which has no basis and no meaning. The polytheists, when he (peace be upon him) recited, would resort to al-muka' (whistling through the hands), al-safir (whistling), al-siyah (shouting), and chanting poetry and rajaz verses (al-ara'ij, a meter of verse). Abu al-Aliyah said: that is, "Find fault with it and disparage it." In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, Abdullah ibn Bakr al-Sahmi, Qatadah, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Sammal, al-Za'farani, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Isa, with a variant (khilaf) from the latter two, read "wa-alghu" with a damma on the ghayn, as the present tense of laghā, which is with a fatha, and both are dialectal forms: it is said laghiya yalgha, like radiya yarda, and laghā yalghū, like ʿadā yaʿdū, when he talks nonsense. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is possible that the fatha reading derives from laghā bi-al-shay' yalghā bihi, when one throws something away, so that ﴿fihi﴾ means "with it," that is, "throw it away and cast it aside." ﴿So that you may prevail﴾, meaning, that you may prevail over him in his recitation, or that you may obliterate his matter and extinguish his remembrance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 27:

﴿فَلَنُذِيقَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ That is: "By Allah, We will surely make these speakers of this (saying) taste..." The use of the apparent noun (alladhina kafaru, "those who disbelieved") in place of the pronoun is to indicate the reason (for the punishment), or it refers to all the disbelievers, and these speakers enter into it as a primary inclusion.

﴿عَذابًا شَدِيدًا﴾ a punishment whose extent cannot be measured. ﴿ولَنَجْزِيَنَّهم أسْوَأ الَّذِي كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ That is, the recompense for the evil of their deeds which are, in themselves, the worst. Here "afal" (aswa') is for absolute intensification (al-ziyadah al-mutlaqah). It is also said that He, glory be to Him, does not recompense them for their good deeds, such as aiding the distressed, maintaining ties of kinship, and hospitality to guests, because these are nullified by disbelief. The punishment is either in both abodes or in one of them. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "a severe punishment" refers to the Day of Badr, and "the worst of what they used to do" refers to the Hereafter.

﴿That﴾ refers to the recompense just mentioned, and it is the subject (mubtada'). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the recompense of the enemies of Allah﴾, is its predicate (khabar). That is: the recompense just mentioned is a recompense prepared for His enemies, exalted is He. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿the Fire﴾, is either an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "recompense," or a substitute (badal), or the predicate of an omitted subject.

It is also permitted that ﴿that﴾ be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is that," with "recompense" (jaza') as the subject and "the Fire" (al-nar) as its predicate. In this case the reference of "that" is to the content of the preceding sentence. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity﴾, is an independent sentence confirming what came before it. It is also permitted that "the Fire" be the subject and this sentence its predicate, meaning that this very place is their abode, with "in" (fi) being used for abstraction (tajrid), as it has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 21], and in the verse of the poet:

*And in God, if they do not deal justly, is a just judge.*

Abstraction is that another thing similar to a described thing is extracted from it, for the sake of exaggerating that attribute. It is also permitted to say that the intended meaning is the mention of the attribute, and that the abode was mentioned only as a preparation, as if it were said: "For them therein is eternity." It has also been said that the statement is on its apparent meaning and the locative sense (zarfiyyah) is literal, and the intended meaning is that for them, in the Fire which contains the levels (darakat), there is a specific abode in which they are abiding. The first interpretation is more eloquent.

Page 120

﴿as a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted in the sense of "they will be recompensed with a recompense," or governed by the preceding verbal noun (masdar), since a verbal noun is put in the accusative by its like, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Hell is your recompense, a full recompense﴾ [Al-Isra: 63]. The first "bi" (preposition) is connected to "recompense," and the second is connected to "yajhadun" (they deny). The second is placed before its verb for the purpose of a relative restriction (qasr idafi), together with its consideration of the rhyme (fawasil). That is: it is because of what they used to deny of Our true signs, not because of matters that ought to be denied. Some have made denial (juhud) a metaphor for the vain speech that results from it, meaning: as a recompense for what they used to speak vainly about Our signs.

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, while they were being tossed about in the punishment that has been mentioned.

﴿Our Lord, show us those two who misled us from among the jinn and mankind﴾. They mean the two groups of devils of both kinds, who were assigned to them as companions and who drove them to disbelief and sins through enticement and adornment. It is reported from Ali, may Allah honor his face, and from Qatada that the two are Iblis and Qabil, for they were the cause of disbelief and of killing without right.

This has been objected to: it is not authentically transmitted from Ali, may Allah honor his face, since Qabil was a believer who committed sin. The apparent meaning is that the disbelievers only asked to be shown those who misled them into disbelief, which leads to eternal abiding in the Fire. That they were the chief of the disbelievers and the chief of the people of major sins is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr read «أرِنا» with a light pronunciation, like «كَفَخْذٍ» with a sukun in «فَخِذٍ» (that is, the vowel of the second letter is dropped, as in the word «فَخْذٍ» for «فَخِذٍ»). In al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary), «أرِنا» is given with a kasra for seeking insight, and with a sukun for asking for a gift, and he transmits this from al-Khalil. According to this reading, the meaning of the recitation is: give us those two who misled us, ﴿that we may place them beneath our feet﴾, trampling them under them as vengeance upon them. It was also said: we will place them in the lowest level of the Fire so that their punishment will be intensified. Thus the intended meaning is that we place them in the direction that is beneath our feet.

In the seven canonical readings, «اللَّذَيْنِّ» is recited with a doubled nun. This is a proof against the Basrans, who do not permit doubling it in this form when it ends with a ya', and likewise in «اللَّتَيْنِ» and «هَذَيْنِ» and «هاتَيْنِ». ﴿So that they may be among the lowest﴾, in humiliation and abasement, or in place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 41, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ This begins an explanation of the good state of the believers in this world and the Hereafter, after the explanation of the bad state of the disbelievers in both. That is, they said it, acknowledging His lordship (*rububiyya*) and affirming His oneness (*wahdaniyya*), as the restriction (*hasr*) implied by the definiteness of both parts of the sentence indicates, as in "my friend is Zayd." ﴿Then they remained steadfast﴾, meaning they held firm to the affirmation and did not revert to polytheism. It is related from al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited this verse, and it was revealed, as is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and then said: "What do you say about it?" They said: "They did not sin." He said: "You have taken the matter to its extreme." They said: "What do you say?" He said: "They did not return to worshipping idols."

And from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "They were steadfast for Allah, the Exalted, by obeying Him; they did not dodge like foxes." From 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "They made their deeds sincere." From Amir 'Ali, may Allah honour his face: "They performed the obligatory duties." Al-Thawri said: "They acted in accordance with what they said." Al-Fudayl said: "They renounced the transient and desired the lasting." Al-Rabi' said: "They turned away from everything other than Allah, the Exalted."

In *al-Kashshaf*, the meaning is: "then they remained firm in the affirmation and its requirements." He intended that whoever says "My Lord is Allah, the Exalted" has acknowledged that He, the Mighty and Majestic, is his Owner, the Manager of his affairs, and his Nurturer, and that he is a servant under the care of his Master. So remaining steadfast on what this entails is that his foot does not slip from the path of servitude, in heart and in body, and that he does not overstep it. All acts of worship and beliefs are included in this. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to someone who asked for a matter to hold on to: "Say, 'My Lord is Allah,' then be upright." He mentioned that what is related from the Rightly Guided Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them, are particular instances of this meaning, each mentioned as an example. It is not hidden that the statement of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, makes it unlikely that what he mentioned was given as an example. Perhaps the "then" (*thumma*) here is for a gradual progression in rank (*al-tarakhi al-rutbi*, the "then" of progression in rank, indicating that the later matter is greater), since steadfastness upon it is greater and harder than the affirmation. The same is said for most of the earlier exegeses. It is also permitted that it is for temporal progression (*al-tarakhi al-zamani*), because steadfastness occurs after a period from the time of the affirmation. And when steadfastness is interpreted as performing the obligatory duties or as action, it is taken as the "then" of progression in rank as well, on the basis that the affirmation is the starting point and source of steadfastness upon it. This is the opposite of the progression in rank you heard about first, because in that case the element joined to is higher in rank than the one joined, as it is the foundation and the basis. In the case mentioned, the element joined is higher in rank than the element joined to, as is not hidden.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾ from Allah, their Lord, the Exalted. ﴿The angels﴾. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "At death." Muqatil said: "At the Resurrection." It is related from Zayd ibn Aslam: "At death, in the grave, and at the Resurrection." It was also said: "The angels descend upon them to support them with what occurs and arises for them of religious and worldly matters, by way of inspiration (*ilham*), what expands their hearts and removes fear and sorrow from them, just as the disbelievers are led astray by the evil companions assigned to them, through the adornment of vices." It was said: "This is the most apparent (view), because of its generality and comprehensiveness, which includes their descent in the three stations mentioned earlier and others." We have already told you that most people say the angels descend upon the pious on many occasions and that they take from them what they take, so reflect on this.

﴿Do not fear﴾ what you are about to face, for fear is a distress that comes from anticipating something disliked. ﴿Nor grieve﴾ over what you have left behind, for grief is a distress that comes upon the occurrence of the loss of a benefit or the arrival of harm. This is related from Mujahid. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "Do not fear the rejection of your good deeds, for they are accepted, and do not grieve over your sins, for they are forgiven." It was also said: "The intent is a prohibition against distress in general."

The meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, has decreed for you safety from every distress, so you will never taste it. The particle *an* (*anna*, the "that" particle) is either a verbal-source particle (*masdariyya*) with *la* as a prohibitive or negating particle; the omission of the nun (*nun*) indicates the subjunctive, and the statement in the form of a report is in the position of a command, for emphasis. Or it is a lightened form of the heavy *inna*, with *tatanazzalu* implying knowledge, and *la* as a prohibitive particle; in both cases *an* is taken to be implied with the meaning of *bi* ("with"), meaning "with (the fact) that you should not fear," or "with the fact that it is (the case that) you should not fear," where the *ha'* is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*). Or it is an explanatory *an* (*mufassira*), with *tatanazzalu* implying the meaning of speech, and *la* also a prohibitive particle.

In the recitation of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud), it is "Do not fear" without *an*, meaning "they say: do not fear," in which case it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the angels, or a resumptive new sentence (*isti'naf*).

﴿And rejoice in the Garden which you were promised﴾, meaning the Garden you were promised in the world through the tongues of the Messengers, peace be upon them. This is among their good tidings at one of the three stations.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 31:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world﴾, to the end of the verse, is among their glad tidings in this world; that is, we are your helpers in your affairs, inspiring you with the truth and guiding you to what is good and right for you. Perhaps this is an expression of what occurs to the believers who persist in acts of obedience, namely that this comes by Allah's Exalted granting of success and support to them through the mediation of the angels, peace be upon them. It is also permissible, according to the view of some people, that the angels say to some of the God-fearing, directly and in other than those situations: ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world﴾ and ﴿in the Hereafter﴾, we will support you with intercession and receive you with honour when there occurs between the disbelievers and their companions what occurs of claims and disputation.

Some exegetes held that this is also among their glad tidings in one of the three situations, in the sense of: we were your allies in the world, and we are your allies in the Hereafter. It was also said that this is from the speech of Allah Exalted, not of the angels; that is, We are your allies with guidance and protection in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And for you therein﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, ﴿is what your souls desire﴾ of the various kinds of delights, ﴿and for you therein is what you ask for﴾, what you wish for. The word is a form of ifti'al from supplication in the sense of request; that is, you ask for yourselves. According to some, it is more general than the first, since requesting may occur in matters that are immaterial and in spiritual, intellectual virtues. It was also said that there is a partial overlap between them, since a person may desire what he does not seek, like the sick person who desires what harms him and does not want it. The claim that wishing is more general than willing is not accepted; yes, it was said: if by what is wished is meant what it is valid to wish for, not what one actually wishes for, then that is different.

Ibn 'Isa said: what is meant by ﴿what you ask for﴾ is that what you claim is yours is yours by the decree of your Lord. (﴿for you﴾) in both places is a predicate, and (﴿what﴾) is a subject, and (﴿therein﴾) is a circumstantial phrase referring back to its pronoun in the predicate. The reason for not being satisfied with conjoining (﴿what you ask for﴾) to (﴿what your souls desire﴾) is to indicate that each of the two stands independently.

﴿نُزُلا﴾ (nuzulan), an accommodation prepared for a guest. Al-Hasan said: (مِنّا) "from Us." Others said: "a reward." Its tanwin (nunation) is for magnification, and so is its qualification by His saying, ﴿مِن غَفُورٍ رَحِيمٍ﴾ "from the Most Forgiving, Most Merciful."

The well-known meaning is that the nuzul is what is prepared for the nazil (the guest), that is, the visitor, so that he may eat it upon his arrival. It is good to take the word in this sense here as a figure of speech, because it points to the greatness of the honour that follows. Its case is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, which refers back to (ما تَدَّعُونَ) "what you ask for." It is not a hal of the omitted pronoun referring back to "what" (ma), because that would corrupt the meaning. The wishing and the claiming do not take place in the state of being a nuzul. Rather, that claimed thing was established for them and settled for them in the state of being a nuzul. To make it a hal of the subject itself is not hidden from anyone with discernment.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: (نُزُلًا) is accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). The transmitted form of the verbal noun of nazala is nuzul (نُزُولٌ), not nuzul (نُزُلٌ). Some took it to be a verbal noun of anzala. It was also said that it is the plural of nazil, like sharif and shuruf, so it is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier as well, meaning "alighting" (nazilin). The dhu al-hal (the entity described by the circumstantial qualifier), according to Abu Hayyan, is the pronoun of the subject in (تَدَّعُونَ) "you ask for." On this view, ﴿مِن غَفُورٍ﴾ cannot be attached to it. It was said that it lies in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in the adverbial phrase. So do not be heedless.

Abu Haywa recited (نُزْلًا) with the zay sukun (silent).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 33:

﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾ That is, to His Oneness (tawhid) and obedience to Him. The apparent meaning is generality, covering every caller to Him, Exalted is He. This is the view of al-Hasan, Muqatil and a group. It was also said that it is specific. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Also from him: they are the companions of Muhammad ﷺ. 'A'isha, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the muezzins (mu'adhdhinun). Their saying should be interpreted so that they are included within the verse, for otherwise the surah in its entirety is Meccan without disagreement, and the adhan was not in Makkah; it was only legislated in Madinah. Committing to the view that its ruling was delayed after its revelation is, as you see, [problematic]. The apparent meaning is that the intended calling is calling by the tongue. It was also said: by it and by the hand, such as calling to Islam and striving (jihad). Zayd ibn 'Ali said: "He called to Allah by the sword." Perhaps this, and Allah knows best, is what moved him to rise up with the sword against some of the oppressive kings of the Banu Umayyah. This Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him, was a scholar of the Book of Allah, Exalted is He, and he had a tafsir which he dictated to some of those who transmitted from him, while he was in the prison of Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, and it contains abundant knowledge and citation of the speech of the Arabs.

It is said that when he and his brother Muhammad al-Baqir debated, people gathered with inkwells, writing down what proceeded from the two of them of knowledge. May Allah have mercy on both of them and be pleased with them.

The interrogative here carries the sense of negation, meaning: no one is better in speech than one who calls to Allah ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾, that is, a righteous deed, whatever righteous deed it may be.

Abu Umamah said: he prayed between the adhan and the iqamah, and what is in this is not hidden. 'Ikrimah said: he prayed and fasted. al-Kalbi said: he performed the obligatory duties, and the truth is generality. ﴿And said: Indeed I am of the Muslims﴾, that is, he uttered that, rejoicing that he is among them and boasting of it, along with intending reward, since that does not contradict it. Or he made Islam his religion and adopted it as his creed, from the saying "this is the saying of so-and-so", meaning his school of thought and belief. Some return both meanings to a single meaning. The meaning, on the view that the verse is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, is that he chose the attribution to Islam over the worldly glory and nobility, and this is their saying "reject; do not listen to this Qur'an", and an expression of astonishment at it. Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibrahim ibn Nuh, from Qutayba al-Mayyal, read "and said (inni)" with a doubled nun, without the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya).

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi used the verse as evidence that the condition of "if Allah wills" (istithna') is not required in the statement of one who says: "I am a Muslim" or "I am a believer". In the verse there is an indication that the caller to Allah, Exalted is He, should be one who acts righteously, so that people will be closer to accepting his call and more at ease with it.

﴿Nor are the good deed and the evil deed equal﴾ is a resumed sentence (*jumlah mustanfa'ah*), brought to explain the excellent deeds that take place between people, following the explanation of the excellent deeds that take place between the servant and his Lord, Mighty and Majestic. It encourages the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to be patient with the harm of the polytheists and to meet their evil with good. The ruling is general: the good trait and the evil trait are not equal in their effects and rulings. The second "nor" (*wa la*) is extra, to emphasise the negation, like it in His saying: ﴿Nor are the shade and the heat﴾ [Fatir: 21], because *istawa* (to be equal) does not suffice with a single term. His saying: ﴿Repel with that which is better﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining the good outcome of the good deed. That is: repel the evil when one of your enemies confronts you with that which is better than it, namely the good deed. This is on the understanding that "the better" means the one that is more excellent absolutely, or "the best of the good deeds by which it can be repelled", such as doing good to one who has done evil, for that is better than mere forgiveness. So *ahsan* (better) is on its literal sense, and the thing it is compared to is general, which is why it is omitted, as in ﴿God is greater﴾. Its being framed as an answer to the question of one who says: "How should I act?" is for emphasis and to indicate that it is important and deserves attention and inquiry. Also for emphasis, *ahsan* (the better) is placed in the position of *hasanah* (good deed), because whoever repels with the better finds it easy to repel with what is lower than it. From what we have mentioned it is known that the good deed and the evil deed do not refer to two specific things.

It is related from ʿAlī, may God honour his face, that the good deed is love of the Messenger and his household, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them, and the evil deed is hatred of them. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that the good deed is "There is no god but God" and the evil deed is polytheism. Al-Kalbī said: "The two calls to them." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Forbearance and obscenity." It was said: "Patience." It was said: "Gentle dealing and harshness." Other things were also said. It is not hidden that some of what is transmitted can hardly be intended here, so perhaps it was not established from those to whom it is attributed. It is also permitted that the intended meaning is to explain the variation of good deeds and evil deeds in themselves, in the sense that good deeds vary into good and better, and evil deeds likewise. Then the definiteness of "the good deed" and "the evil deed" is generic, and the second "nor" is not extra, and *afʿal* (better) is on its literal sense. The statement of ﴿repel﴾ and what follows is in the sense of "then" (*fa*): that is, if each of the two kinds varies in its individual instances in itself, then repel with the better of the two good deeds against the evil and the worse. The "then" is omitted for the resumption we mentioned, which is the stronger of the two connections. Perhaps the first is closer.

﴿Then, behold, he between whom and you there is enmity will be as though he were a warm friend﴾ is an explanation of the result of the repelling that was commanded. That is: when you do that, your hostile opponent becomes like a sincere, compassionate friend. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: The particle *ka-anna* (as though), which conveys comparison, has entered, because an enemy does not truly become a warm friend by repelling with what is better; rather, his outward appearance becomes good, so he is likened to a warm friend. Perhaps this is from the category of suffice with the least of what is necessarily implied. This is according to what usually happens; otherwise enmity may entirely disappear by that, as has been said:

*Enmity transforms into affection,*
*by making up for lapses with good deeds.*

And ﴿he between whom and you there is enmity﴾ is more eloquent than "your enemy", and for that reason it was chosen over it despite its length. It was said that the verse was revealed concerning Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, who was a manifest enemy of the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him. Then he became, according to the People of the Sunnah, a sincere friend. It seems that what was with him passed to the son of his son, Yazīd, and God, Mighty and Majestic, gave him what he deserves.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 35:

﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ That is, "none is granted (yulaqqa) and given (yu'ta) this deed and this noble trait, which is repelling evil with that which is better." The pronoun refers to what is understood from the context. It has also been permitted that the pronoun refers to "that which is better" (allati hiya ahsan). Makki reported that the pronoun refers to the testimony that there is no god but Allah, so that it returns to "that which is better," and it has been explained as the testimony mentioned. Yet this, as you see, is weak. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to Paradise, but this is not correct.

Talhah and Ibn Kathir, in one narration, read «وما يُلاقاها» from al-mulaqah (encounter). ﴿إلا الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾ That is, those who have within them the nature of patience and its character. ﴿وما يُلَقّاها إلا ذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمٍ﴾ "Possessor of a great portion" means a great share of the qualities of goodness and perfection of the soul, as narrated from Ibn Abbas. Qatadah said: "Possessor of a great share" means a great share of reward. It has also been said: "the great share" is Paradise. According to these two views it is a promise; according to the first it is a praise. ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ is repeated as an emphasis on praising that beautiful and sublime deed, and for the unique person of his age, whom time has been stingy in bringing the like of, Salih Afendi, secretary of the Diwan al-Insha' in al-Hadba'. In this verse there is a concise expression, whose precision was observed by God's mercy upon him, namely His saying: ﴿وما يُلَقّاها إلا الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾, the verse. It is possible to derive from the first part what is from the first of the first, not the second, because of agreement; thus the most noble is realized after giving the situation its due, so the restrainer realizes that he is favored and stops at the defined limit. End of quotation.

And Allah knows best what he intended: it is possible to derive from the first, namely His saying: ﴿وما يُلَقّاها إلا الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾, and from the second, which is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وما يُلَقّاها إلا ذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمٍ﴾, what figure it is from the first of the four forms of the first figure. It is a syllogism composed of two universal affirmative premises, producing a universal affirmative conclusion, by saying: "Every patient one is the one who is granted it, and everyone who is granted it is a possessor of a great share," producing: "Every patient one is a possessor of a great share." A syllogism cannot be derived from the second figure because the premises agree in quality, and the condition of the second figure is that the two premises differ in it, as is established in its place. Thus, after taking and composing the two premises, the more noble matter is realized, namely the conclusion, which is a universal affirmative, and it is the most noble of the four quantified propositions, because it includes the more noble affirmation over negation, and the universal is more noble than the particular, after giving the situation its due by making the relative pronoun express totality, as was pointed out, so that it conveys universality. At that point it is realized, and the restrainer, that is the patient one, knows that he is favored, that is possessor of fortune and portion, so he stops at the defined limit and does not go beyond patience to anything else. Understand.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 36:**

﴿And if an incitement (*nazgh*, a prodding or stirring up to evil) from Satan should afflict you, then seek refuge in God﴾. *Al-nazgh* is *al-nakhs*, which is touching with the tip of a stick or a finger with a painful force. It is used here metaphorically for the whispering that prompts toward evil, and the verb is made to act as an agent (*nazighan*) for emphasis, in the manner of *jadda jidduhu* ("his fortune was great"). On this reading, *min* (من) in ﴿min al-shaytan﴾ is *ibtida'iyya* (indicating the starting point). It is also permissible that *nazigh* be intended as a noun, with the verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle as a description of Satan. In that case *min* (من) is *bayaniyya* (explanatory), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). Alternatively, *min* may again be *ibtida'iyya*, but in the mode of *tajrid* (abstraction, where the described thing is treated as if it were a separate entity). It is also permissible that *al-nazigh* means Satan's whispering, with *in* (إنْ) as a conditional particle and *ma* (ما) as a superfluous particle (*mazida*), meaning: "And if Satan incites you and diverts you from what you were enjoined to do, namely repelling evil with what is better," ﴿then seek refuge in God﴾ from his evil, and do not obey him. ﴿Indeed He﴾, may He be exalted and majestic, ﴿is the All-Hearing﴾, so He hears your seeking refuge, may He be glorified, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, so He knows your intention and your righteousness, may His majesty be exalted. It was also said: "All-Hearing of the words of the one who harmed you, All-Knowing of his deed, so He will take vengeance on him, relieving you of the need to avenge yourself." It was also said: "All-Knowing of the incitement of Satan." Making the abandonment of repelling (evil) one of the effects of Satan's incitements serves as an additional warning and a call to keep away from him. Perhaps the address here is of the kind of the verse:

*It is you I mean, so listen, O neighbour.*

It is also permissible that *al-shaytan* be intended to include the devil of mankind, for among them are those who are diverted from repelling evil with what is better, and who say:
Page 125
"He is your enemy, who did to you such-and-such and such-and-such. So seize the opportunity against him and take your revenge on him, so that you may be great in his eyes and in the eyes of the people, and so that weakness, lack of resolve, and indifference are not attributed to you," and other such phrases which perhaps never occur to the mind of a jinn-devil. We seek refuge in God, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from every devil.

ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd explained *al-nazgh* as anger. The verse is cited as evidence for the recommendation of seeking refuge (*al-isti'adha*) at the moment of anger.

Al-Hakim narrated from Sulayman ibn Surad, who said: "Two men reviled each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the anger of one of them intensified. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'Indeed, I know a word which, if he said it, the anger would leave him: *I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.*' The man said: 'Do you think I am insane?' Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And if an incitement from Satan should afflict you, then seek refuge in God﴾."

Perhaps anger is among the effects of the whispering.

[Ruh al-Ma'ani, Tafsir of al-Alusi, on Surah 41, verse 37]

﴿And of His signs﴾, which indicate His exalted majesty, may His glory be great: ﴿the night and the day﴾ in their coming into being and their succession, and in the entering of each of them into the other. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾ in their giving of light, and in their differences in the strength of light, size, effects and movements, for example. The night is mentioned first, it is said, to draw attention to its precedence, even though darkness is a non-existence. The mention of the sun after the day is appropriate, because the sun is its sign and the cause of its illumination, and because it is the source of the light of the moon, according to what they have said, that the moon's light is derived from the light of the sun. As for the sun's own light, the well-known view is that it does not come to it from another body. It is also said that it comes from the Throne. The philosophers of today think that it comes from another body, and they claim that they see in one part of the body of the sun a small darkness. ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun, nor to the moon﴾, because they are among the created things of Allah, glory be to Him, which are subjected to His will, like you. ﴿But prostrate to Allah, who created them﴾. The pronoun is said to refer to the four mentioned things, and the intention is to attach the act to the sun and the moon. However, the night and the day were arranged together with them to indicate that they belong to the category of things that do not know and do not choose, since the night and the day are necessarily of this kind. Had the pronoun been dual, there would have been no such indication.

The ruling on a group of non-rational things, according to what al-Zamakhshari said, is the ruling of the feminine, so one says: "the pens, I have sharpened them" (bariytuha) and "I have sharpened them (feminine plural)" (bariytuhunna). So it should not be imagined that, since the pronoun refers to the night, the day, the sun and the moon, it would be more appropriate to give precedence to the masculine. The answer that, since they are among the signs, they are treated like feminines, is a strained answer, and there is no need for it because of the rule mentioned. Yes, Abu Hayyan said: one should distinguish between the plural of paucity (jam' al-qilla) among these and the plural of abundance (jam' al-kathra), for the more eloquent usage in the first is that the pronoun be singular feminine: one says "the trunks (al-ajdha') broke" (inkasarat), which is the more eloquent usage; in the second the more eloquent usage is that the pronoun be feminine plural: one says "the trunks (al-judhu') broke" (inkasarna). What occurs in the verse is not a plural of paucity with a singular form, but it is treated as if it were the thing referred to by it. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the sun and the moon, and the dual is a plural, and the plural of non-rational things is treated as feminine. And from the point where one says "suns" (shumus) and "moons" (aqmar), because they differ by days and nights, it is permissible for the pronoun to refer to them in the plural. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the signs mentioned earlier in His saying, may He be exalted: (And of His signs, if you truly worship Him). Prostration is the highest degree of worship, so it must be specified for Him alone, may He be mighty and majestic. ʿAli, may Allah honor his face, and Ibn Mas'ud prostrated at (you worship). The view that this is the place of prostration is attributed to al-Shafi'i. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Wa'il and Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah prostrated at ﴿they do not tire﴾. Likewise it is narrated from Ibn Wahb, Masruq, al-Sulami, al-Nakha'i, Abu Salih, Ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin and Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Tahrir attributes this to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. In al-Kashf, the more correct of the two views according to our companions, meaning the Shafi'is, is that the place of prostration is ﴿they do not tire﴾, as is the position of Imam Abu Hanifa. Its reasoning is that it completes the meaning in the style of "prostrate!", since refusing it is blameworthy. Some have justified it on grounds of caution: if it is at (you worship), postponing it is permissible because the separation is short; but if it is at ﴿they do not tire﴾, it is not permissible to hasten it.

[p. 126]

﴿But if they are arrogant﴾: they magnify themselves against abstaining from what they were forbidden, which is prostrating to those created things, and against carrying out what they were commanded, which is prostrating to their Creator. So let them not concern you, or let that not diminish the greatness of your Lord. ﴿Then those who are with your Lord﴾: that is, in the presence of His holiness, Exalted and Majestic is He, from among the angels, upon them be peace, who are better than them ﴿glorify Him night and day﴾: that is, constantly, even though for them there may be no night or day. ﴿And they never tire﴾: they do not grow weary of that. The true answer to the conditional (jawab al-shart, the apodosis of the conditional clause) is what we have pointed to or something similar to it, and what has been mentioned stands in its place. It is also permissible that the statement be meant as a declarative, as has been said regarding a phrase like "if you honour me today, then I have honoured you yesterday," that it means "so I inform you that I have honoured you yesterday."

It was read as «لا يِسْأمُونَ» with a kasra on the ya' (yi'). The apparent meaning is that the verse concerns some disbelievers who used to prostrate to the sun and the moon, like the Sabians in their worship of the stars, and who claimed that by prostrating to them they intended prostration to God Most High. So they were forbidden this intermediary, and they were commanded to direct their prostration to the Face of God Most High, sincerely.

Shaykh Abu Ishaq used this verse in al-Muhadhdhab (a major work of Shafi'i jurisprudence) as evidence for the prayers of the solar and lunar eclipses. He said: "Because there is no prayer connected with the sun and the moon other than these two." And from this it was derived that these two prayers are preferred over the prayer for rain (salat al-istisqa'), because the sun and the moon are mentioned in the Qur'an while the prayer for rain is not.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 39:

﴿And among His signs is that you see﴾ O you to whom sight is possible: ﴿the earth humbled (khashi'ah)﴾, meaning dry and flattened, a metaphor borrowed from khushu' in the sense of submissiveness. ﴿Then when We send down water upon it﴾, i.e., rain, ﴿it stirs and swells (ihtazzat wa rabat)﴾, i.e., it moves with vegetation and expands, because when a plant is about to emerge, the earth rises for it and swells, then it splits open for the plant. It is also possible that the expression contains an allegorical metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), in which the state of the earth's barrenness and its emptiness of vegetation, then God's giving it life by rain, its transformation from barrenness to fertility, and its producing every lovely pair, is likened to the state of a person who is dejected, downcast in spirit, shabbily dressed, and held in no regard; then, when he obtains some of the goods and adornments of this world, he takes pains with all kinds of ornament and embellishment, so he struts in his walk out of pride, and sways with his limbs out of vanity and arrogance. Thus the likened element (al-mushabbah) is omitted, and khushu' and ihtizaz are used as indications of its place. The reading that considers the metaphor as allegorical is preferred. It is also read ﴿rabatʾ﴾ (with hamzah), meaning it increased. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of rabat is it became great, and rabaʾat with hamzah means it rose, and from it comes al-rabiyyah, which is a lookout posted on a high place. ﴿Indeed He who gave it life﴾ with what has been mentioned after its death ﴿(is surely the One who gives life to the dead)﴾ through resurrection, ﴿indeed He is over all things﴾ among things, of which giving life is one, ﴿Powerful (qadir)﴾, with emphasis on power.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 40:**

﴿Indeed, those who distort (yulhidun) regarding Our verses﴾ deviate in the interpretation of the verses of the Qur'an from the direction of soundness and uprightness, so they bear them upon false meanings. This is the meaning intended by Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) in his saying: "They place speech in other than its proper place." Its root is from *alhada* (ألحد), meaning that one inclined away from uprightness, so he dug in a crevice (*shaqq*), and it is said *lahada* (لَحَدَ). It has been read as *yalhadun* (يَلْحَدُونَ) and *yulhidun* (يُلْحِدُونَ), in both dialects. Qatadah said: "Here, *al-ilhad* is denial (*al-takdhib*)." Mujahid said: "It is whistling, clapping, and idle talk." So the meaning is that they incline away from what is fitting and proper regarding Our verses, so they either deny the Qur'an or engage in idle talk and whistle while it is being recited. It is also permissible that the verses be understood as including all the revealed books, and *ilhad* as including altering and changing the wording; but this applies to other than the Qur'an, since that did not happen to it as it happened to other books, as is the common view. It is also transmitted from Abu Malik that "verses" here means proofs (*al-adilla*), so *ilhad* regarding them is to attack their indication and to turn away from them. This is more fitting with the words of the Exalted:

﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled…﴾ etc. And what preceded is more fitting with His words, glorified be He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it"﴾ [Fussilat: 26] and what follows it. The verse, according to the interpretation of Mujahid, is more fitting and even more fitting.

The meaning of His words, the Exalted: ﴿They are not hidden from Us﴾ is that He will requite them for their distortion; so the verse is a threat and a warning to them. His words, the Exalted: ﴿Is he who is cast into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ are an indication of the manner of the recompense. The apparent expectation was that casting into the Fire would be contrasted with entering Paradise, but He departed from this to what is in the sublime composition, out of concern for the state of the believers, because security from punishment is more general and more important. For this reason, in the first part the expression "cast" (*al-ilqa'*) is used, which indicates compulsion and subjugation, and in the second part "coming" (*al-ityan*) is used, which indicates that it is by choice and contentment, together with security and entry into Paradise. This does not preclude that their state be changed after their fear into security. It is also permissible that the verse is an instance of *ihtibak* (الاحتباك, a rhetorical device in which corresponding elements are omitted from each part), with the implied meaning: "Is he who comes fearful and is cast into the Fire, or he who comes secure and enters Paradise?", so that from the first is omitted the counterpart of the second, and from the second the counterpart of the first. But this is a remote interpretation. As Ibn Bahr said, the verse is general, covering every disbeliever and every believer.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Is he who is cast into the Fire﴾ that it refers to Abu Jahl, and ﴿or he who comes secure﴾ refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). Abd al-Razzaq and others transmitted from Bashir ibn Tamim: "'He who is cast into the Fire' is Abu Jahl, and 'he who comes secure' is Ammar, and the verse was revealed concerning these two." Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and Uthman ibn Affan. It was also said: concerning him and Umar. It was said: concerning him and Hamzah. Al-Kalbi said: concerning him and the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿Do what you will﴾ is a severe threat to the disbelieving, distorting ones who are cast into the Fire, and the intended meaning is not the literal command. ﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾, so He will recompense you according to your deeds.
