Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 41:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿when it has come to them﴾, without any time passing over them in which they might reflect upon it and consider it, ﴿and indeed it is a Book of might﴾, meaning one whose like is not found, or one that is invincible, such that opposing it cannot be achieved. The root of ʿizz (might) is a state that prevents a person from being overcome, and its application to the absence of a like is a well-known metaphor, and likewise its being invincible. It has also been said: it prevails over the (other) books, because it abrogates them. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: that is, honoured with God Most High. And the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), conveying the extreme heinousness of disbelief in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 42:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Falsehood cannot come at it from before it or from behind it﴾, is another attribute of the Book. "What is before it and what is behind it" is a metaphor (kinayah) for all directions, like "morning and evening" as a metaphor for all time. The meaning is that falsehood cannot reach it from any of its directions. In this there is also an image (tamthil), likening it to a person protected from all sides, so that his enemies cannot reach him, because he is in a fortified stronghold of the protection of the Manifest Truth. It is also permitted that the meaning is: falsehood cannot come at it from the direction of what it reports of past reports and future matters.

It has been said: "al-batil" (falsehood) is used in the sense of "al-mubtil" (the one who nullifies), like kawāris in the sense of mūris, or it is a verbal noun like al-ʿāfiyah in the sense of mubtil, also. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy﴾, means: praiseworthy for the blessings He has bestowed, of which is the sending down of the Book. His praise, glory be to Him, is realized through the tongue of the state (lisan al-hal) from every one who is blessed, and through the tongue of speech (lisan al-qal) from whoever has been granted success in that. It is either the predicate of an omitted subject, or another attribute of "Book" conveying its grandeur through annexation (al-fakhamah al-idafiyyah), just as the two preceding attributes convey its grandeur in its essence (al-fakhamah al-dhatiyyah).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Falsehood cannot come at it﴾ .. etc. is an interjected clause (i'tiradh) according to those who do not permit placing a non-explicit attribute before an explicit one. All of this is to emphasize the nullity of disbelief in the Qur'an.

They differed concerning the predicate of ( inna ), whether it is mentioned or omitted.
Page 128
It has been said: it is mentioned, and it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are called from a far place﴾. This is the view of Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla, in an account that took place between him and Bilal ibn Abi Burdah. Bilal was asked about this in his assembly and said: "I have not found a way through it." Abu ʿAmr said to him: "Indeed it is near to you: ﴿Those are called from a far place﴾." Al-Hawfi also held this view, and it is in a far place. Abu Hayyan held that it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Falsehood cannot come at it﴾, with the returning pronoun omitted, i.e., "the disbelievers," and the state of it is that it is a mighty Book, falsehood cannot come at it from them; that is, whenever they seek to nullify it, they do not reach it. Or by making "al" in "al-batil" a substitute for the pronoun, according to the view of the Kufans, i.e., its falsehood does not reach it. Or it is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿What is said to you﴾ .. etc., and the returning pronoun is also omitted, i.e., what is said to you concerning them or about them, except what was said to the messengers before you, i.e., was revealed to you concerning these who deny you and what you have brought, like what was revealed to those messengers before you, namely that their end will be evil: in this world by destruction, and in the Hereafter by everlasting punishment. Then he said: The most that can be said of these two explanations is the omission of the returning pronoun, while it is present, as in "the ghee is two manns for a dirham" and "the wheat is a kurr for a dirham," meaning "from it."

It is reported from some Kufan grammarians that the predicate is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty Book﴾, and he (Abu Hayyan) criticized this, saying that it is not conceivable. It has been said that it is omitted, and the predicate of ( inna ) may be omitted when the meaning is understood. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar asked ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd about this, and ʿAmr said: "Its meaning in interpretation is that those who disbelieved in the Reminder when it came to them, they disbelieved in it, and indeed it is a mighty Book." ʿIsa said: "You have done well, O Abu ʿUthman." Some said: its estimate is "obstinate" or "doomed." Al-Kisa'i said: what preceded it of speech before it has filled its place, namely His saying: ﴿Is then he who is cast into the Fire﴾; as if he meant that it is omitted and indicated by what precedes it, so it may be estimated as "they abide in the Fire." The predicate may be estimated, as Ibn ʿAtiyyah preferred, after "Praiseworthy." In al-Kashshaf it is said that it is His saying: ﴿Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿Indeed those who distort Our verses﴾. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: he did not explicitly address whether the predicate of ( inna ) is mentioned or omitted, but he may claim that he alluded to it, for what is predicated of the substituted-from is what is predicated of the substitute, so the estimate would be: "Indeed those who distort Our verses — indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it came to them are not hidden from Us."

In al-Kashf, the benefit of this substitution is to alert that what drives them to distortion is only mere disbelief, and it conveys a warning against the aspects of what was mentioned, and placing "the Reminder" in the position of the pronoun returning to the verses is an added humiliation for them; and what is in "lamma" conveys their surprise at disbelief the first moment it came, and what it contains of glorifying the status of the verses, and a preparation for speaking of the perfection of the Book, which indicates the evil outcome of one who distorts it. Then, the more likely reading is that the words of al-Kashshaf are to be understood as meaning that the predicate is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and for added terror, so that the mind goes every way; and the clause is a substitute for the clause, because substitution by repeating the governing word is only permitted with a genitive noun, due to the strength of the connection. End of quote. So reflect. And God Almighty is the Granter of success.

This is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the harm he suffers from the disbelievers, such as their attacks on his Book and other things. The one who says it is the disbelievers, meaning: what the disbelievers of your people say about you and about the Qur'an that has been revealed to you. ﴿Nothing is said to you except what has been said﴾, meaning like what the disbelievers before you said ﴿to the messengers before you﴾, of hurtful speech that contains attacks on what was revealed to them. This is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus no messenger came to those before them except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 52].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Owner of forgiveness and the Owner of painful punishment﴾, it has been said that it is a reason (ta'lil) for what is derived from the context concerning the command to patience, as if it were said: What is said to you is only like what was said to the likes of you among the messengers, so be patient as they were patient. ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Owner of great forgiveness﴾ for His friends ﴿and the Owner of painful punishment﴾ for their enemies; so He supports His friends and takes revenge on their enemies. Or it is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: Then what? So it is said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Owner of forgiveness﴾ for His friends ﴿and the Owner of painful punishment﴾ for their enemies. He has indeed supported, for this reason, those messengers before you, peace be upon them, and took revenge on their enemies, and He will do the same for you and against your enemies as well.

It is also permissible that the speaker is Allah, exalted is He, and the meaning, according to what I have heard from Abu Hayyan, and he made this sentence the predicate of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed). That is: What Allah, exalted is He, reveals to you concerning the disbelievers who harm you is only like what He revealed to the messengers before you concerning the disbelievers who harmed them, namely that their end will be evil in this world by destruction and in the Hereafter by painful punishment. So be patient; indeed your Lord... etc. And ﴿Indeed your Lord...﴾ etc. may be taken, with regard to its content, as an explanation of what is said. The essential meaning is: What was revealed to you and to the messengers was only the promise to believers of forgiveness and to disbelievers of punishment, not the reverse which the disbelievers claim by the tongue of their state. So be patient, for Allah, exalted is He, will fulfil His promise.

It has also been said that what is said is the laws (shara'i'), meaning: what is revealed to you is only like what was revealed to the messengers of the laws, not matters of this world. The custom of the disbelievers has been to deny that. So what does it matter to you if the disbelievers of your people deny it? Be patient over that. Some have made ﴿Indeed your Lord...﴾ etc. a reason for that as well. Some have made it an explanation of that said thing, namely the laws, because they are the divine commands and prohibitions, and these are summarized in it. There is in this much remoteness, and Qatada went to something similar to what we mentioned first.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said concerning the verse: ﴿What is said to you﴾ of denial ﴿except what has been said to the messengers before you﴾. So just as they were denied, you are denied; and just as they were patient over the harm of their people towards them, be patient over the harm of your people towards you.

The choice of ﴿alim﴾ (painful) over ﴿shadid﴾ (severe), although it is more fitting with the verse endings (fawasil, the rhyme-ends of verses), is to hint that the composition of the Qur'an is not like rhymed prose (saj') and sermons, that its beauty is intrinsic, and that attention in it is directed to the meanings rather than the words. And describing the punishment with it here is fitting, since the punishment is the requital of denial, which is painful.

[p. 130]

**"Had We made it an Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, 'Why are its verses not clearly explained?'"** This is a response to their saying, "Why was the Qur'an not revealed in the language of the non-Arabs?" The pronoun refers to the Reminder (*al-dhikr*). ﴿They would have said, "Why have its verses not been made distinct?"﴾, meaning: why have they not been explained and made clear to us in a tongue we understand?

As for His statement, ﴿Is it a non-Arabic (scripture) and an Arab (recipient)?﴾, it is read with two hamzas: the first is the interrogative hamza, and the second is the hamza of *a'jamiyy*. The majority read it with an interrogative hamza followed by a *madda*, which is the hamza of *a'jamiyy*. This is a rhetorical denial that establishes the force of the reproach (*tahḍīḍ*). The meaning is: "Is it a non-Arabic speech while the messenger, or the one addressed, is Arab?" The upshot is that if it had been revealed as they wished, they would have objected in this way too, saying, "What have you to do with non-Arabic?" or "What have we to do with non-Arabic?"

*A'jamiyy* is originally *a'jam* without a *yā'*, and its meaning is one whose speech is not understood, either because of a speech impediment or because of the strangeness of his language. The *yā'* is added for emphasis, as in *aḥmariyy* and *dawwāriyy*. It is applied to his speech metaphorically (*majāz*), but the usage became so common that it came to be treated as literal. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* (a work on the Qur'anic readings) claimed that the *yā'* in it is like the *yā'* in *kursiyy*, but this is a mistake.

It has also been said that "*'Arabiyy*" [in the second reading] may mean "and the one addressed is Arab," though the addressees are plural, so the correct form would have been *'arabiyyah* or *'arabiyyūn*. This is because the intention is to show the contradiction and incongruity between the speech and the one addressed, not to specify whether the addressee is singular or plural. It is incumbent on an eloquent speaker to keep his speech focused on what it is intended to convey, and not to add anything beyond what strengthens it. If he sees a long garment on a short woman, he says, "The garment is long and the wearer is short," not "the wearer [feminine] is short," because the statement does not concern the masculinity or femininity of the wearer. If he had said the latter, one would imagine that this has a bearing on what the speech is about. This is one of the principles that must be kept in mind, and on which omission and mention, restriction and generality, and other features are based, in the speech of God Most High and in every eloquent speech.

ʿAmr ibn Maymūn read *a'jamī* with an interrogative hamza and a fatḥa on the ʿayn, meaning: "Is it a speech attributed to the non-Arabs?" The non-Arabs are all who are not Arabs, though the term may also be restricted to the people of Persia and their language, which is also called *al-'ajamiyyah*. Thus there is a general and particular relation of partial overlap between *al-a'jamiyy* and *al-'ajamiyy*.

The apparent meaning of "*'Arabiyy*" in the well-known reading is the opposite of "*a'jamiyy*," and in the other reading its opposite is "*'ajamiyy*."

Al-Ḥasan, Abū al-Aswad, al-Jaḥdarī, Sallām, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn ʿĀmir, with variant reports from the last two, read *a'jamiyy* without an interrogative and with a sukūn on the ʿayn. On this reading the statement is an assertion that the Qur'an is non-Arabic, while the speaker or the addressee is Arab.

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "Why have its verses not been made distinct, so that some of them are non-Arabic to make the non-Arabs understand, and some of them Arabic to make the Arabs understand?" This was transmitted from Ibn Jubayr. On this reading the sentence is a predicate of an omitted subject: some of it is non-Arabic and some of it is Arabic. The purpose of the conditional clause is to refute their proposal, namely that it be in the language of the non-Arabs, by showing that it entails an undesirable consequence, namely the defeat of its purpose. For there is no sense in revealing it in a non-Arabic tongue to someone who does not understand it. Or the point is to show that they will never cease their obstinacy: when the non-Arabic is provided, they demand something else, and so on.

﴿Say﴾, in reply to them: ﴿It is, for those who believe, a guidance﴾ leading to the truth, ﴿and a healing﴾ for what is in the breasts of doubt and dubiety. ﴿As for those who do not believe﴾, it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿in their ears is a deafness﴾. This is one way of parsing it: "*fī ādhānihim*" is the predicate placed first, and "*waqr*" is the subject, meaning: "there is in their ears a deafness," that is, a heaviness that prevents them from hearing it. It has been said that the predicate of the relative clause is "*fī ādhānihim*," and "*waqr*" is the agent of the adverbial phrase. It has also been said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is "it is the verses of the Qur'an," and "*fī ādhānihim*" is related to the omitted element that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of "*waqr*." This last is preferred because it corresponds better with His statement, ﴿and it is for them a blindness﴾. He who permits coordination of a word with two governing elements coordinates the second relative clause with the first, and "*waqr*" with "*hudan*," so that the sense is: "It is a guidance for those who believe, and for those who do not believe it is a deafness." His statement ﴿in their ears﴾ is mentioned either as an explanation of the location of the deafness, or as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, which refers back to "*waqr*." The first is more eloquent. But this is objected to, because of the remoteness of the view that neglects what is disputed in permitting that kind of coordination, since it involves making the Qur'an itself the deafness, especially as its location has been mentioned. This is unlike making it the blindness itself, because blindness is the opposite of making it the guidance itself, so the antithesis is preserved, which is why its location is not specified. As for deafness, if the Book is made the deafness itself, it is like an intrusion and does not correspond to what occurs elsewhere in the revelation. This objection also applies to the previous view. Ibn al-Ḥājib, in *al-Amālī*, permitted that ﴿and it is for them a blindness﴾ be connected to His statement, ﴿It is, for those who believe, a guidance and a healing﴾, the estimate being: "It is for those who believe a guidance, and for those who do not believe a blindness." His statement, ﴿Those who do not believe, in their ears is a deafness﴾, is a parenthetical clause interposed between the invocation (of the believers and the disbelievers). This was criticized: although it may be permissible grammatically, it is rejected in terms of meaning, because it disrupts the structure of the discourse.

Some have claimed that the pronoun in "*huwa*" refers to the deafness, and that it is a part of blindness, but this is as you see.

The best of these views is the first one mentioned. The preposition *'alā* is used in ﴿upon them a blindness﴾ to indicate that blindness has overwhelmed them. The heart's condition is not mentioned, because it is already understood from the implicit reproach in His statement, ﴿for those who believe it is a guidance and a healing﴾, that for others it is a grievous disease.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the second relative clause, in view of its being characterized by what is in the scope of its relative clause. The demonstrative *ulā'ika* carries the sense of distance, to indicate how far their rank is in wickedness, and it is also fitting for the calling from a far place. The meaning is: those far-off ones, characterized by what has been mentioned, namely deafness (*al-taṣāmm*) to the truth that they hear, and blindness to the signs that they see. ﴿They are called from a far place﴾ is an image of their failure to understand and to benefit from what they are called to, like someone called from a distant place, who hears the voice but does not grasp its details or meanings, or who neither hears nor understands. The lexicographers recorded that one says to someone who does not understand: "You are being called from afar." This meaning is also transmitted from ʿAlī, may God honour his face, and from Mujāhid. It is also related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that the statement is literal, and that on the Day of Resurrection they will be called by their unbelief and their evil deeds, by their most abominable names, from far away, so that the people of the assembly hear it, which will bring them shame and disaster.

The summary of the response is that it is a guidance for believers, a healing for what is in their breasts, and sufficient to repel doubts. Therefore it came in their own tongue, miraculous in itself and clarifying for others. Those who do not believe are cut off from benefiting from it, in whatever state it came to them.

Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, Muʿāwiya, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and Ibn Hurmuz read *ʿamin* with a kasra on the mīm and with tanwīn. Yaʿqūb al-Qārī and Abū Ḥātim said: "We do not know whether they put tanwīn or pronounced the *yā'* with a fatḥa, as a past-tense verb." It is related without tanwīn by ʿAmr ibn Dīnār and Sulaymān ibn Qutayba from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 45:**

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, but disagreement arose concerning it.﴾ This is a resumed statement, brought to explain that disagreement over the scriptures is an ancient practice among the nations and is not specific to your people, following the line of His saying, ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ [41:43], as you heard earlier. That is: and by Allah, We certainly gave Moses the Torah (Tawrah), but disagreement arose concerning it. Some confirmed it and some denied it. The situation of your people is likewise regarding what We have given you of the Qur'an: some believe in it and some disbelieve. ﴿And had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord﴾ concerning your denying nation, namely the promise to postpone their punishment and to defer the dispute between them and the believers until the Day of Resurrection, similar to His saying, ﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time﴾ [54:46], and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿But He delays them until a specified term﴾ [35:45], ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ by the annihilation of the deniers, as was done to the deniers of the earlier nations. ﴿And indeed they are﴾, that is, the disbelievers of your people, ﴿in doubt concerning it﴾, that is, concerning the Qur'an, ﴿disquieting﴾, meaning causing unease and agitation. It was also said: the second pronoun refers to the Torah and the first to the Jews, by the indication of the context, since they are the ones who disagreed about the Book of Moses, peace be upon him. But this is of no account.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 46:

﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾, by believing in the Books and acting in accordance with what they require, ﴿it is for his own self﴾, meaning: he does it for his own self, or its benefit is for his own self and not for anyone else. (Man) (مَن) may be read in it as both a conditional particle (shartiyyah) and a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and likewise in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾, its harm falls on him and not on others. ﴿And your Lord is not ever a wrongdoer to the servants.﴾ This is an interjected concluding clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyili), confirming the content of what precedes. It is based on treating the withholding of reward from the doer of good for his deed, or the rewarding of another for someone else's deed, and the punishing without fault or for another's fault, as a form of injustice, which is impossible for Him, Exalted. Some scholars did not need this interpretation. The discussion of that, and of the direction of the negation and its emphasis, has already passed, so recall it.

The twenty-fourth part is complete. It is followed by the twenty-fifth part, whose beginning is ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾... etc.

To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. That is, when one is asked about it, it is said: "Allah, exalted is He, knows," or "None knows it but Allah, Mighty and Majestic." The purpose of this statement is to guide the believers in how to respond to this question. Both answers imply that knowledge of it belongs exclusively to Him, exalted is He. As for the second answer, this is evident. As for the first, when you are asked about a matter and you say, "So-and-so knows it," this contains an implicit negation of your own knowledge and an indication that so-and-so is more fitting to be asked about it than you.

﴿Nor does any fruit come out of its husks﴾. That is, from their containers. Akmam is the plural of kimm (with a kasra), meaning the container of the fruit, as in "the spathe (ṭal'a) was enclosed in its sheath (kimm)" when it covered it. It may also be pronounced with a damma. Kumm al-qamis (with a damma) means the sleeve of a shirt. Al-Hasan in one narration, al-A'mash, Talha, and more than one of the Seven Readers read "min thamara" (from a fruit), intending the genus, and the plural form is used because the kinds differ. It was also read "min thamarat" (from fruits) with "min akmamihinna" (from their husks), with the pronoun in the plural. Ma is negative. The first min is extra (ziyada), for emphasizing the comprehensiveness of the negation and making it explicit. The second min is for the starting point (ibtida'iyya). Likewise is "ma" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor does any female conceive or give birth﴾, that is, her pregnancy. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except with His knowledge﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The ba' indicates accompaniment or concomitance. The exception is from the most general of circumstances. That is: no occurrence of the emergence of a fruit, nor of the conception of a pregnant woman, nor of the giving birth of one who gives birth, takes place, connected or accompanied by anything, except that it is accompanied or connected by His all-encompassing knowledge, glorified is He, occurring in accordance with its relation to it. It is also permitted that in the first case the word be a relative pronoun (mawsula) coordinated with "the Hour," meaning: to Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of what emerges. The first min is explanatory (bayaniyya), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The second min remains as it is. The feminine form of ﴿takhruju﴾ is according to the meaning, since ma here means "fruit." It was said: that is not permissible in the second case because of the presence of the exceptive construction with a missing antecedent (istithna' mufarragh). Some have permitted it. The negation in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor does she give birth﴾ suffices for the validity of the missing-antecedent construction. The clause "nor does she give birth" is either a circumstantial clause or coordinated with the clause ﴿To Him is referred﴾, etc. It is not hidden from you that the most apparent in both positions is negation. Then, the exception relates to all of them, and clarifying the common element shared among the three verbs, and making it the basis for the dependency of the missing-antecedent construction, as you have heard, is for the clarification of the meaning and to indicate that in such a case there is no need to omit anything from the first two, namely "what emerges" and "what is carried." This is close to the style of the line of poetry:

"Between the mare and its leaping has been placed a barrier."

Because "kharaja Zayd" means "the emergence of Zayd occurred," just as the meaning of that is "the act of placing a barrier." This is not from the category of the exception that follows multiple sentences (al-istithna' al-muta'aqqib li-jumal), and the disagreement concerning its dependency is about something other than the missing-antecedent construction. The grammarians mentioned it in the chapter on tanazu' (the dispute over a shared element). If it is negated with illa, then the omission is nothing but that. And if it were from that, it would not be among the points of disagreement, because the sentences are unified in purpose and the indication of return to the whole is evident. The discussion, according to what is in Sharh al-Ta'wilat, is connected to the matter of the Hour and the Resurrection, for none knows all of this except Allah, exalted is He. So He mentioned these matters because of their relevance to the knowledge of the Hour, and because all of it is an origination after non-existence by His power, Mighty and Majestic is He. Thus it is like proof for the Gathering. It has also been permitted that it be connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day﴾, etc., and to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled﴾, etc. The meaning then is: among the signs of His divinity and power, exalted is He, is that fruits come forth, females carry, and give birth according to His knowledge, glorified and exalted is He. The first is closer.

﴿And on the day He will call to them: "Where are My partners?"﴾. That is, according to your claim, as He specified by His saying, glorified is He: "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"
[Quoted in the text]

In this there is mockery of them and reproach to them. "Yawm" (day) is in the accusative, governed by "udhkur" (remember), or it is an adverbial complement of an implied, delayed verb which has been omitted, as an indication that explanation falls short of it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when Allah gathers the Messengers﴾. The pronoun in ﴿yunadihim﴾ is general, covering everyone who worshipped other than Allah, exalted is He, so the worshippers of idols are included in it.

﴿They will say﴾, that is, those who are called out, ﴿"We have informed You"﴾, that is, "We have made You aware." The meaning of informing here is telling, because He, exalted is He, is all-knowing, so it is not valid to inform Him of what He, glorified is He, already knows. Unlike telling, which applies to one who knows, it is as if it were said: "We have told You." ﴿"That none of us is a witness"﴾, that is, that none of us testifies to them of being partners. So the clause is in the position of an object (mafʿul) of ﴿adhannaka﴾. It has been noted that it is suspended (ta'liq), and there is disagreement regarding the suspension in the verbs of "a'lama" (to inform) and "anba'a" (to report). The correct view is that it is heard in eloquent usage. ﴿Witness﴾ is on the pattern fa'il, from testimony (shahada). The negation of testimony is a metonymy for disavowal of them, because the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection once denied worshipping other than Him and once acknowledged it, and disavowed it at another time. Al-Samarqandi explained it as denying their worship of other than Allah, exalted is He, and their association (of partners) as a lie and fabrication from them, like His saying, exalted is He, quoting them: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. The apparent meaning of ﴿adhannaka﴾ implies that the announcement preceded in answer to "Where are My partners?" They were asked a second time so that they answered that the answer had already been given, because this is a rebuke, and in the repetition of the rebuke there is the emphasis of the gravity of the offense and the condemnation of the state of one who commits it, which is not hidden. Abu Hayyan deduced that the intended meaning is the creation of an announcement, not a report of an earlier announcement, in the manner of "I divorced" and similar expressions. It has also been permitted to say that it is a report of a prior notification, and that prior notification is what He, exalted is He, knew of their inner states on the Day of Resurrection, that they had not remained upon polytheism and upon that testimony. It is as if it were an announcement from them by the tongue of their state. This does not require any prior question or answer, and in it there is good manners, as if they were saying: "You know it best," and then they proceed to the answer.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: This aspect is the preferred one, because it contains the aforementioned subtle point, and avoids the bad manners found in the other interpretations. It is possible that the meaning is: "We have informed You that none of us sees them," so "shahid" is from "shuhud" in the sense of presence and seeing. The negation of their seeing is apparently literal, and that is in one station, and the case of some of the worshippers being affirmers of their deities in another station, so there is no contradiction between them. It has also been said that it is a metonymy for the negation that He, exalted is He, has any partner, like your saying: "We do not see for you an equal," meaning "there is no equal to you, so that we may see him." The speech regarding ﴿adhannaka﴾ is according to what we have informed You. It has also been said: the pronoun in ﴿qalu﴾ refers to the partners, meaning: the partners said, "None of us is a witness who testifies for them that they were righteous," so "shahid" is from testimony only, and the intended meaning is disavowal of them. In this there is a shifting of pronouns.

The meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And what they used to invoke before has lost them﴾, according to what has been said, is that their associates whom they used to invoke before and hope for benefit from have vanished from them. This is on the basis that *ḍalāl* (going astray, being lost) is in its literal sense, which is the opposite of finding (*wijdān*). Or it means that their associates did not benefit them in any way, on the basis that *ḍalāl* is a figurative (*majāz*) expression for non-benefit. Here *mā* is a relative pronoun referring to the associates. Using *mā* rather than *man* for both rational and non-rational beings is appropriate in this context. It has also been permitted that *mā* refers to the statement they used to make about the associates, that they are gods and partners of God, exalted and glorified be He. The meaning would then be: they forgot what they used to say about their associates, ascribing divinity to them. You may also make *mā* a verbal-noun (*maṣdariyyah*) construction. The clause may be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) or a parenthetical interjection (*i'tirāḍ*). Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that the latter is definite on the view that the pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ refers to the associates and that *ḍalāl* is figurative for non-benefit, so reflect on this.

﴿And they thought﴾, i.e., they were certain, as al-Suddi and others said, because no other meaning is possible here. *Ẓann* often has the sense of knowledge (*ʿilm*). ﴿They have no escape﴾, i.e., no place of refuge. Apparently the clause is in the place of the accusative, occupying the position of the two objects of *ẓanna*, and it is suspended from it by the negative particle. It has been said that the speech is complete at His saying ﴿And they thought﴾, and that *ẓann* retains its apparent meaning: it was dominant in their minds that their saying ﴿None of us bears witness﴾ would be a means of salvation for them, or a matter they used to deceive. The following clause is then a new sentence: they will have no refuge or place of escape.

[Page 4]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 49:

﴿Man does not tire of asking for good⦆ — that is, he does not grow weary or slacken — ﴿from supplication for good﴾ — that is, from seeking abundance in blessing and the means of livelihood. (Du'a', "supplication") is a verbal noun (masdar) in the genitive construction, with its object being the agent; its subject (fa'il) is omitted, meaning: from his supplication for good (i.e., he asks God for good).

ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read (min du'a'in bil-khayr), with a bi' (ba', "with/for") attached to al-khayr (the good).

﴿But if evil touches him﴾ — hardship and difficulty — ﴿then he is despairing, hopeless﴾ — that is, he is despairing and desperate of God's bounty and mercy. This is the attribute of the disbeliever. The verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and it was said: concerning ʿUtba ibn Rabi'a.

His despair is intensified in two respects: in terms of form, since fa'ul is one of the intensive patterns (sighat al-mubalagha); and in terms of semantic repetition, for qunut (despair) means that the trace of hopelessness appears upon him, so that he shrinks and is broken. Since its outward sign that indicates it does not leave him, mentioning it again (after yaʾus) carries a more emphatic mention. He placed yaʾus first because it is an attribute of the heart, namely that he cuts off his hope of good, while it is the one that has the apparent effect on the outward appearance, in the form of shrinking and breaking.

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after some hardship had touched him﴾, meaning: if We relieve him with health after illness, or ease after hardship, or otherwise, ﴿he will surely say, "This is mine"﴾, meaning: it is my due, which I deserve because of my merit and my work, not a bounty from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So the lam (al-lam, the lam of entitlement, lam al-istihqaq) indicates deserving. Or it means: it is mine always and will not cease, so the lam indicates ownership (lam al-milk), and this conveys permanence. The first is closer to the meaning.

﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come﴾, meaning: will be established in what is to come. ﴿And even if I am returned to my Lord﴾, supposing its occurrence, ﴿I will surely have with Him the best (al-husna)﴾, meaning: the best state of honour. The emphasis by oath here is not about the coming of the Hour, but about his being rewarded with the best, by his deserving honour, since he believes that what befell him of the blessings of this world is due to his deserving it, and that the blessings of the Hereafter are likewise. There is no contradiction between the fact that the particle inna (inna, the emphatic particle) is originally used for those other than the God-fearing, and its use here with the oath, with inna and the lam, with the fronting of the two adverbial phrases (al-zarfayn), and with the comparative form (sigha al-tafdil, the elative form). ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, meaning: We will make them know the reality of their deeds, and We will make them see, contrary to what they believed about them, so that it becomes clear to them that they deserve humiliation, not honour, as they had imagined. ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, from which they cannot escape because of its intensity; it is like a thick bond that cannot be cut.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 41, verse 51:**

﴿When We bestow favour upon man, he turns away﴾ from gratitude, ﴿and withdraws with his side﴾ meaning he becomes arrogant and vain. This is on the basis that *al-janib* (the side) means the direction and place. Then the expression "to put the side of a thing in place of its direction" is a *kinayah* (metonymy, an allusive expression) for the thing's very self. From this comes the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿for him who fears the standing of his Lord﴾, and the words of the poet:

*I startled with it the sand-grouse and removed from it the place of the wolf, like the accursed man.*

And the words of the secretaries: "the presence (*hadrah*) of so-and-so and his high assembly (*majlis*)", and "I wrote to his direction and to his noble side," meaning his person and his self. So it is as if it were said: "he withdrew with his self," and then he used his self as a *kinayah* for arrogance and conceit. It is also permissible that *bi-janibihi* means "his flank," and that it be an expression for deviation and turning away, as they say: "he bent his flank" and "he turned away with his corner." The first (interpretation) contains two *kinayahs*: placing the side in the position of the self, and expressing extreme arrogance with something like "he went off with himself." This is one *kinayah* according to what is in *al-Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari). Some of them made *al-janib* and *al-janb* literal, like the flank as a body part and one side of the body, and figurative for the direction. So pay attention. And from Abu 'Ubaydah: "he withdrew with his side" means if he rose up with it, and this is an expression for arrogance, like "he lifted his nose." The *ba'* (with) is for transitivity.

Then, the expression for the person's essence by means of things like *al-maqam* (standing) and *al-majlis* (assembly) is frequently used for the purpose of exalting and showing reverence, rather than naming the person explicitly, and they avoid stating it explicitly when intending to honour him. Zuhayr said:

*So allude when you come to the camp and the sanctuary, and beware lest you forget and mention Zaynab.*

*Her indication will suffice you from that named one; so leave her guarded in majesty, veiled.*

From here al-Tibi said: what is here is addressed as sarcasm (*tahakkum*). And it was read *wa-naa* (with the alif inclined and the nun kasra for harmony), and *wa-naa'a* by inversion (*al-qalb*, transposition of letters), as they said *ra'a* for *ra'a* in the sense of seeing. ﴿And when harm touches him, he has long supplication﴾, meaning abundant and continuous, borrowed from that which has a wide breadth (*ard*). Its origin is from what is used to describe bodies, and breadth is the shorter of the two extensions, while the longer is length. In common usage, "broad" is understood as extensive. The intensive form and the *tanwin al-takthir* (the nunation indicating abundance) strengthen this. Describing the supplication with what has been mentioned also necessarily implies great length, since it must be greater than the breadth, otherwise it would not be length. The metaphor is permissible in both the supplication and the "broad," and how it is applied is not hidden.

Some eminent scholars mentioned that the verses contain two kinds of the excess of mankind. The first is in showing the intensity of his greed for accumulation and the intensity of his distress at loss, and an allusion to wronging his Lord, glorified is He, in His words ﴿this is mine﴾, incorporating within it his evil belief regarding the Return, which draws all those evils. The second is in showing his frivolity, which produces his self-admiration and arrogance when blessing is present, and his humility when it is lost. In this is included a censure of him for being occupied away from the Benefactor in both states. As for the first, it is evident. As for the second, the supplicating in distress over loss is not a return to the Benefactor, but rather grief over a loss that occupies one entirely away from the Benefactor. It was mentioned that in the mention of the two attributes there is an indication that he lacks *nuhyah* (intellect), i.e. is weak in *minnah* (strength), i.e. power, for despair and hopelessness contradict the broad supplication, and that in that state he is like the drowning man who clings to everything. End of quote. From this the answer is known to what was said: that his supplicating broadly and repeatedly contradicts his being described as one who despairs and is hopeless, because supplication is a branch of hope and expectation, and despair is conditioned on the manifestation of the effect of despair, so the appearance of what indicates hope rejects it. Others answered that it is permissible to say: the second state is the condition of some, not the other part about which despair and hopelessness were related, or it is the condition of all at some times. Some used the words of the Exalted ﴿so one of broad supplication﴾ as proof that *al-ijaz* (brevity) is other than *al-ikhtisar* (abridgement). He interpreted it, for this verse, as omitting the repetition of speech with the unity of meaning, and *al-ijaz* by omitting its length, which is *al-itnab* (amplification). This is an argument from what does not prove it, since there is no omission of that breadth in it, let alone naming it.

[p. 5]

﴿Say: Have you considered?﴾ etc. is a return to the reproach of the critics and the atheists, and a conclusion of the surah with what turns back to the beginning of it. It is from the even-handed speech, and in it is an urging to reflection and a drawing toward acknowledgment, along with what it contains of the magic of eloquence. The mention of the Hour occurred in between, as a completion of the threat and an alert to what they are in of far-reaching error, so it is said. There will come, if God the Exalted wills, an exposition of this matter.

The meaning of ﴿Have you considered?﴾ is: inform me. ﴿If it be﴾, i.e. the Qur'an, ﴿from God, then you disbelieve in it﴾ despite the converging reasons requiring belief in it. And ﴿then﴾, as al-Nayisaburi said, is for the sequence of rank. ﴿Who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition﴾, i.e. dissension, ﴿far﴾, extremely far from the truth. What is meant by "one who is in opposition" is the addressees, and the apparent noun was placed in the position of their pronoun, explaining their state by the relative clause and giving a reason for their increased error.

The clause ﴿who is more astray﴾, according to Ibn al-Shaykh, stands in the place of the two objects of "ra'aytum". In al-Bahr, the first object is omitted, its estimate being "have you considered yourselves", and the second is the interrogative clause. In either case, the answer of the condition is omitted. Al-Nayisaburi said: its estimate, for example, is "then who is more astray among you?" It was also said: "If it is from God and you disbelieve in it, then inform me who is more astray among you", and this is probably the more apparent.

[p. 6]

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We shall show them Our signs on the horizons﴾ and so on, is connected, according to what the author of al-Kashshaf (*al-Kashshaf*, the exegesis of al-Zamakhshari) chose, to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Tell me﴾ and so on, by way of *tatmim* (completion, supplementing a point) and *irshad* (guidance), toward what it contains of urging reflection, so that it may lead to the purpose: that they may be guided to its inimitability (*i'jaz*), believe in what it brought, act upon its requirements, and attain complete success.

He explained the signs as the conquests (*futuhat*) that Allah, exalted is He, brought about through the hands of His Prophet (ﷺ) and through the hands of his caliphs and companions, may Allah be pleased with them, which demonstrate the strength of Islam and its people and the weakness of falsehood and its party. *Al-afaq* (the horizons) are the regions; the singular is *ufuq*, with two *damma*s, or *afaq* with two *fatha*s. That is, "We shall show them Our signs in the regions in general, from the easts and wests of the earth, and its north and south." In this is the indication that this showing is certain to occur, a truth about which no doubt hovers.

﴿And in themselves﴾: in the lands of the Arabs specifically. This is the *atf* (coordination) of Jibril (Gabriel) upon his angels. In turning from *fi al-afaq* to *fi anfusihim* lies what is not hidden: establishing that victory, confirming its significance as evidence for the truth of what is to be proven, and showing that its being a sign concerns the selves, even though its being a conquest concerns the land and the town.

﴿Until it becomes clear﴾, that is, becomes manifest, ﴿to them that it﴾, that is, the Qur'an, is ﴿the truth﴾, the one ﴿falsehood cannot approach from before it or from behind it﴾. So it is entirely the truth from Allah, exalted is He, who knows every unseen and witnessed thing. Therefore those who carry it were made victorious, and they were in the right. In the definite form there is a grandeur and magnificence that is not hidden, in majesty and rank.

In what has been mentioned is an indication that He, exalted is He, does not cease to produce conquest after conquest and sign after sign, until He makes it (the religion) prevail over all religion, even if the polytheists dislike it. Consider this comprehensive verse, how it indicated the truth of the Qur'an in a manner that included the truth of its people and their victory over the opponents. And how excellent is that as consolation for what the preceding verse suggested of their immersion in falsehood to a degree that nearly approaches despair.

It was said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger (peace be upon him), or to the religion, or to monotheism, but the first is likelier.

﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) coming to rebuke them for their denial of the realization of the showing.

The hamza is for denial, and the waw, according to one of the two opinions, is for coordination with an assumed element that the hamza entered upon, which the context requires. The *ba'* is extra for emphasis, and "Your Lord" is the subject (*fa'il*) of *kafa*. The addition of the *ba'* to its subject is the well-known opinion, the one approved by the grammarians. It is also added to the subject of the verb of wonder (*fi'l al-ta'ajjub*), as in *ahsin bi-Zayd* ("how well Zayd does"), for *ahsin* is a past verb put in the form of the imperative, the *ba'* is extra, and Zayd is the subject according to a group of grammarians. It is hardly ever added to anything other than these two.

And his saying:

*Did it not come to you, while the news is spread about what the camels of the sons of Ziyad encountered?*

This is, according to al-Shihab, rare and ugly.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that He is over all things a witness﴾, is a *badal* (apposition) from the subject, a *badal al-ishtimal* (comprehensive apposition). It was said that it is with an assumed preposition, that is: "Is it not sufficient for them that your Lord [witnesses] that He..." And the grammarians' discussion of this type of construction is well known. That is, they denied the showing of that, which indicates the truth of the Qur'an, and it was not sufficient as evidence for them that He, mighty and majestic, has knowledge of every thing and is aware of it, and of their state and your state, which necessitate the wisdom of your victory over them and their abandonment. It seems that because this is evident, it was treated as though it were known to them.

In *al-Kashf* (the commentary of al-Tibi): that is, "Is it not sufficient for them that your Lord, glory be to Him, has knowledge of every thing, for unseen things and witnessed things are equal to Him," in the sense of: "Is it not sufficient for them that this showing is a decisive proof?" And since what He promised was unseen to them, how, when it has descended while they are in a state of weakness and scarcity, suffering what they suffer from the polytheists of Makkah? It was said: "Is it not sufficient for them that the knowledge of Him who revealed this true Book, of every unseen and witnessed thing, is a proof of the existence of the showing and the bringing of that unseen before them, since there is no unseen with respect to Him, exalted is He?" In the turn to this expression there are two benefits. The first is the confirmation of the fulfilment of that promise, as though it were witnessed, by mentioning the decisive proof of its occurrence. The second is the indication
[p. 7]
that this showing, now, while they are in weakness and scarcity, has been accomplished with respect to establishing the truth of the Qur'an. For whoever knows that He is a witness over all things, and knows that the Qur'an is inimitable from Him, knows that all that is in it is truth and sincerity, and so knows that that victory will occur.

The summary is that just as one derives from those signs the truth of the Qur'an and the truth of its people, at another time one derives from the inimitability of the Qur'an the truth of those signs as occurring, and the truth of the people of Islam at another time. Thus the two meanings were expressed in one comprehensive phrase that accomplishes both aims in a manner that cannot be more complete. There is no concealing that in this verse there is a kind of riddle (*ilghaz*).

It was said: that is, "Has He not made them independent of the showing of the promised signs, which clarify the truth of the Qur'an, and was it not sufficient for them in that that He, exalted is He, is a witness over all things, and He has informed that it is from Him, mighty and majestic?" And this, as you see, is weak.

It was said: the meaning is, "Was it not sufficient for you that He, exalted is He, over all things is one who realizes it, so He will realize your affair by manifesting the promised signs, as He realized the other promised things?" It was objected that, along with its implying what does not befit the greatness of the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely hesitation concerning the realization of the promised matter as mentioned, this does not suit

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 41, verse 54 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾. That is, they are in great doubt about it, that is, about the Resurrection, because they deem it far-fetched that the dead should be restored after their parts have scattered and their limbs have separated. So they do not give heed to the proofs that would benefit them at their meeting with Him, exalted is He, such as the truth of the Qur'an, for it explicitly states that lack of sufficiency is considered with respect to them.

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Unquestionably, He encompasses all things﴾ serves to explain what follows from that doubt. This is based on the meaning that He, exalted is He, knows all things in the most perfect manner, so nothing hidden from them escapes Him, majestic is He and exalted. Therefore He, majestic is His majesty, will certainly requite them for their disbelief and their doubt.

It has also been said: it repels their doubt and their skepticism about the Resurrection and the restoration of what has scattered and become mixed, which they imagine cannot be distinguished. That is, He, exalted is He, knows the totalities of things and their details, and has power over them, and nothing of them escapes Him. Glorified is He, Who knows the parts and is able to resurrect.

Furthermore, what has been mentioned in the interpretation of ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾ in the sense narrated from al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu al-Minhal and a group, who said: His saying, glorified is He, ﴿We will show them﴾ and so on, is a warning to the disbelievers of what Allah, exalted is He, will open to His Messenger (ﷺ) from the regions around Mecca and elsewhere on earth, such as Khaybar. By His saying, exalted is He, ﴿within themselves﴾ He meant the conquest of Mecca. Al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: ﴿on the horizons﴾ refers to what befell the denying nations in the regions of the earth in former times, and ﴿within themselves﴾ refers to what happened on the day of Badr, for in that there is evidence of the victory of those who brought the truth and were denied among the prophets, peace be upon them, and so it indicates the truth of the Prophet (ﷺ) and what he brought of the Qur'an. It has been objected that ﴿We will show them﴾ rules out that what is on the horizons is what befell the denying nations, since it was already visible to them before. ʿAtaʾ and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons﴾ is the regions of the heaven and the earth, of the sun, the moon, the rest of the stars, the winds, the lofty mountains and other things, and ﴿within themselves﴾ refers to the subtle workmanship and wondrous wisdom. The Imam (al-Razi) criticized this with something similar to what you have just heard. It has been answered that although the people had seen those signs, the wonders that Allah, exalted is He, has deposited in them are without end. So He, glorified is He, makes them aware of these wonders in a near time, state after state. For everyone sees the structure of the human being, yet the wonders deposited in its composition cannot be counted, and most people are heedless of them. So whoever is moved to reflect upon them through the revelatory warnings and divine admonitions, the more he reflects, the more he is brought to stand (in awe). Thus the meaning of the future tense is sound.

The author of al-Kashshaf chose this interpretation, following others, and explained how the verses relate to what precedes them. He made the pronoun in ﴿that it is the Truth﴾ refer to Allah

, majestic and exalted is He, saying: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah﴾, there is an indication that its being from Him, glorified is He, contradicts disbelief in it, and that they accept this, but they challenge its being from Him, majestic is He and exalted. Therefore, the phrase ﴿the tales of the ancients﴾ was made in reply to their saying ﴿What has your Lord sent down?﴾, that it is a turning away from its being sent down and an answer that it is tales and not something sent down. So it was intended to establish that it is truly from Him, exalted is He, by way of metonymy, so that it would be more effective in reaching the aim and would fit what the discourse is built upon, namely the path of fairness. Thus it was said: ﴿We will show them﴾, that is, Allah, exalted is He, will show them. The shift (from the first person) is to indicate greater specificity and to affirm the certainty of the showing. Then it was said: ﴿until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth﴾, that is, that Allah, majestic is His majesty, is the Truth from every aspect: in His essence, attributes, speech and action, and all else is false from every aspect; there is no truth except Him, glorified is He. When His truth, exalted is His majesty, becomes clear to them from every aspect, it necessarily follows that the Qur'an is established and that it is from Him, exalted is He, by necessity. Then it was said: ﴿Is it not sufficient that your Lord…﴾, that is, is it not sufficient for you that His witnessing over all things? For from Him, glorified is He, you witness all things, not from the signs of the horizons and the selves witnessing Him, exalted is He. The first is reasoning from the effect to the cause, and the second is from the cause to the effect. This is what is called the lammi ʿaynī (the demonstration from effect to cause, in its proper sense). In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿your Lord﴾ with its pronoun referring to him (ﷺ), and in preferring it over ﴿Is it not sufficient with Him﴾, there is an indication that he, peace and blessings be upon him, and those who follow him from among all the knowers of God, are the ones for whom His witnessing over all things suffices as proof, and that this is for them the very care and nurturing of Him, exalted is He, without any role of their own in learning it, unlike the first (group). Then it was said: ﴿Indeed, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾, therefore His being a witness over all things does not suffice for them, because they have no witnessing by which they could witness His witnessing, exalted is He. So it includes both groups, the righteous and the disbelievers. As for the disbelievers, it is because they are in doubt about the very principle. As for the righteous, it is because they are in doubt about the witnessing, that is, they have no knowledge of it except a faith purely derived from imitation.

The use of "doubt" (mirya) is a generalization (taghlib), and the appropriateness of its placement is not hidden. Then it was said: ﴿Unquestionably, He encompasses all things﴾ as a completion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is it not sufficient with your Lord﴾, because whoever encompasses all things in knowledge and power, nothing escapes his witnessing. So whoever witnesses Him witnesses all things. This is the way of generalizing the verses without restricting them to the conquests, and it is more fitting than the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid. He followed the principles of the Sufis and the scholars of the fundamentals, may God's mercy be upon them all. The end. But the meaning has gone far from this, and has over-strained itself. The knower al-Jami, sanctify his secret, in his Nafahat, transmitted from al-Qashani that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will show them﴾ and so on indicates the unity of being (wahdat al-wujud). I have seen in some books of that group the use of this verse as evidence for that, and making the pronoun in ﴿that it is the Truth﴾ refer to the seen thing, and interpreting ﴿the Truth﴾ as Allah, majestic and exalted is He. From this and similar things, the Greatest Shaykh (Ibn al-ʿArabi), may God sanctify his secret, said: Glory be to Him who manifested things while He is their very essence. And this unity is that in which understandings have been bewildered, and necks have slipped out of the noose of Islam due to the failure to verify its matter. The Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, may God sanctify his luminous secret, has several treatises on verifying the truth in them and establishing its foundations. We ask God, exalted is He, to bestow upon us the sound witnessing and to protect us by His generosity from what has clung to the minds of the heretics of the unity of being.

It is read (innahu ʿala kulli shayʾin shahid) with a kasra on the hamza of inna, implying an omitted "saying" (idmar al-qawl). Al-Sulami and al-Hasan read (fi muriyah) with a damma on the mim, which is a dialect of it like the kasra. Similarly (khufyah) with a damma or kasra on the kha; the kasra is more common, for the sake of harmony with the ya.

Among the sayings of this group on the verses: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is a reward never cut off﴾. In it there is an indication that the reward of the believer who does not act is cut off, that is, diminished in comparison with the reward of the believer who acts. The reward of this active one for physical deeds, such as prayer and pilgrimage, is Paradise; for heart deeds, such as contentment and trust in God, it is longing and love and sincerity of seeking; for spiritual deeds, such as turning toward Allah, exalted is He, it is the unveiling of secrets, the witnessing of meanings, intimacy with Allah, exalted is He, and aversion from creation, and miracles; for the deeds of the secrets, such as turning away from all else completely, it is the continuance of manifestation. ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One Who created the earth﴾

that is, the earth of humanity, ﴿in two days﴾, the two days of desire and nature, ﴿and you set up rivals to Him﴾ from among desire and nature, ﴿and He placed in it firm mountains﴾, the human intellects, ﴿and blessed in it﴾ with the five senses, ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾ from the human powers, ﴿then He rose to the heaven﴾, the heaven of the heart, ﴿and it was smoke﴾, a divine primary matter, ﴿so He completed them as seven heavens﴾, which are the seven states of the heart. The first is the place of whispering; the second is the locus of passing thoughts; the third is the source of vision, and is called the fu'ad (inner heart); the fourth is the spring of wisdom, and is called the qalb (heart); the fifth is the mirror of the unseen, and is called the suwayda (the inner black spot of the heart); the sixth is the abode of love, and is called the shaghaf (the covering of the heart); the seventh is the place of manifestation of self-disclosure, the center of secrets and the descent place of lights, and is called the habba (the seed). ﴿In two days﴾, the two days of the human spirit and inspiration, ﴿and We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾, which are the lights of remembrances and acts of obedience. ﴿Indeed, those who said: Our Lord is Allah﴾, on the day they were addressed with "Am I not your Lord?", ﴿then remained steadfast﴾ upon their affirmation when they emerged into the world of forms, and did not deviate from it like the hypocrites and the disbelievers. This is because steadfastness varies: the steadfastness of the common people is outwardly in commands and prohibitions and inwardly in faith; the steadfastness of the elite is outwardly in turning away from the world and inwardly in turning away from Paradise, out of longing for the Merciful; the steadfastness of the elite of the elite is outwardly in observing the rights of the pledge by surrendering self and wealth, and inwardly in annihilation and subsistence. ﴿The angels descend upon them﴾ with descents that vary according to their ranks. It is reported from some imams of the Household (ahl al-bayt) that the angels crowd upon us with their mounts, or something to this effect. ﴿And rejoice in the Garden which you were promised﴾. It too varies: among them is one who is given glad tidings of the known Garden, and among them is one who is given glad tidings of the Garden of union and the vision of the Exalted King. ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾ by abandoning all else, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ so that his state does not contradict his words, ﴿and says: Indeed I am of the Muslims﴾, those who submit to His judgment, content with His decree and destiny. In this there is an indication of the qualities of the guiding shaykh and what he should be, and what should be said of many of those who presume to guide in this age, whose waves are churning with corruption:

The papers have become empty of the rukhakh (a chess piece), and the pawns have been promoted in them,
And the lame donkeys have neighed, and that is from the lack of the thoroughbreds.

﴿And good and evil are not equal﴾. Good is turning toward Allah, exalted is He, with sincere seeking and purity of love; evil is seeking other than Him and contentment with the base. ﴿Repel with that which is better﴾, which is seeking Allah, exalted is He, and seeking nothing other than Him, glorified is He. ﴿Then he between whom and you there is enmity﴾, who is the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara bi al-su'), ﴿will be as though a devoted friend﴾, through the purification of the self from its blameworthy qualities and its weaning from reprehensible transgressions. ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan incites you﴾, to incline toward what it desires, ﴿then seek refuge in Allah﴾ and return to Him, glorified is He, lest its incitement affect you. In this there is an indication that one should not feel secure from deception, nor be heedless of Allah, majestic and exalted is He. ﴿Indeed, those who distort concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us﴾. In this there is an indication of the evil of those who deny the saints, for they are among the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and denial is a form of distortion. We ask Allah, exalted is He, for pardon and well-being. ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and a healing﴾, that is, the Qur'an, according to their ranks. Among them is one whom it guides to the witnessing of the All-Knowing King. Thus, from the truthful one (al-Sadiq), upon his fathers and upon him be peace: Allah, exalted is He, has indeed manifested Himself in His Book to His servants, but they do not perceive. ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾. In this there is an indication that creatures do not see the signs except by His showing them, majestic and exalted is He. This showing is the unveiling of veils, so that it becomes clear that the entities have never smelled the fragrance of existence and never will, and that He, majestic and exalted is He, is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, "Allah was, and nothing was with Him, and He is now as He was." To this they point with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth﴾. And from here the Greatest Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, said:

Adam is not in existence, nor is Iblis, nor the kingdom of Solomon, nor Bilqis.
[p. 10]
All is indication, and you are the meaning, O you who to hearts is a magnet.

Most of his speech, may his secret be sanctified, is of this kind. Rather, he is the mother of *wahdat al-wujud* (the unity of existence), its father, its son, and its brother. Beware lest you say as that most exalted one said, until, by God's grace, you reach what he reached. God, Mighty and Majestic, is the guide to the straight path.

The commentary on the surah is complete. Praise belongs to God for His abundant blessings. Blessings and peace be upon His Messenger Muhammad, the manifestation of His names, and upon his family, his companions, all his followers and beloved ones, with blessings and peace that endure until the Day of meeting Him.
